articles.title: Amazon lays off 121 workers across corporate and fulfillment jobs in Washington state
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Amazon is cutting 121 jobs in Washington state, according to a new state regulatory filing on Monday, hitting corporate tech teams in Bellevue and Seattle as well as fulfillment operations in Sumner.

The largest single concentration of cuts is at the SEA106 building in Bellevue, where 49 employees — ranging from entry-level software development engineers and applied scientists to a vice president of legal and senior software managers — were notified.
In Seattle, impacted positions span multiple downtown office buildings and include roles such as a director of human resources, product managers, and technical writers.
Beyond corporate offices, 32 positions were cut at the BFI1 fulfillment center in Sumner, affecting warehouse associates, service technicians, and safety specialists.

“Teams across the company regularly review their structures to ensure they’re best set up to deliver on their goals,” Brad Glasser, an Amazon spokesperson, told GeekWire via email. “As part of these reviews, teams sometimes determine that certain roles are no longer necessary. We don’t take these decisions lightly, and we’re always committed to supporting employees whose roles are impacted by them.”

The Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) filed with the state’s Employment Security Department says impacted employees were notified between July 1 and July 29 and terminations will be effective between Oct. 1 and Oct. 27.
Amazon says it provided 90 days of advance notice, during which affected workers can apply for open internal transfer positions before separations become final.

Amazon employs roughly 50,000 corporate and tech workers in the Puget Sound region, divided between its primary headquarters in Seattle and its growing operational footprint in Bellevue. Across Washington state, the company employs more than 80,000 total workers across corporate offices, data centers, and fulfillment hubs.
Earlier this summer, Amazon cut 57 jobs in Washington. Those layoffs followed cuts of 2,198 Washington-based employees in February and 2,303 in October 2025 .
The previous larger cuts were part of an effort to “reduce layers, increase ownership, and remove bureaucracy,” according to a memo sent to employees.

A number of layoffs across the tech sector have impacted Washington employees in recent months, including at Microsoft, Zillow, Meta, Google, T-Mobile, Salesforce, Starbucks, TikTok, Qualtrics and elsewhere.

articles.title: Seattle-area biotech led by ex-Athira CEO Leen Kawas raises $35M for hepatitis D drug
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: A Kirkland, Wash.-based biotech company led by former Athira Pharma CEO Leen Kawas has raised $35 million in a Series A round led by Propel Bio Partners , the Los Angeles investment firm where Kawas is a co-founder and managing general partner .

EIT Pharma said Monday that the oversubscribed round also drew participation from Good Ventures, Arrowtown and others. The company said the money will support FDA review of lonafarnib, an oral treatment candidate for chronic hepatitis D, along with manufacturing and commercial preparations, subject to regulatory approval.
The Food and Drug Administration accepted the company’s New Drug Application for review on Aug. 11.

Lonafarnib came to EIT Pharma through the 2024 bankruptcy of Eiger BioPharmaceuticals , in a court-supervised sale that closed that September. The same sale included peginterferon lambda, which EIT Pharma is developing for severe respiratory infections.

Kawas, EIT Pharma’s CEO, said in a news release Monday that the oversubscribed round validates the company’s founding belief that “advancing important medicines is about recognizing unrealized potential.”

Chronic hepatitis D is a serious liver disease that affects people who are already infected with hepatitis B. The FDA approved the first U.S. treatment for chronic hepatitis D in May: Gilead’s injectable Hepcludex, or bulevirtide-gmod. EIT Pharma is positioning lonafarnib as a potential oral alternative, if approved.

Kawas resigned as CEO of Athira Pharma in 2021 after a board investigation found she had altered images in research she co-authored as a graduate student. She said at the time that the changes were enhancements that did not alter the underlying data.
Athira has since changed its name to LeonaBio and shifted its focus from Alzheimer’s disease to breast cancer.

articles.title: Redfin fills CEO role with former Meta VP Alessio Sanfilippo after acquisition by Rocket
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Redfin , the Seattle-based real estate brokerage acquired last year by Rocket Companies, has named Alessio Sanfilippo as CEO.

Sanfilippo was previously Meta’s vice president of insights for Reality Labs, where he led teams working in data science, data engineering and user research to develop the company’s AI-enabled wearable glasses. He earlier served as a VP for Meta-owned WhatsApp overseeing data and user research.

Rocket, the nation’s largest mortgage lender, bought Redfin in a deal worth $1.75 billion. The Redfin brand kept its name and Seattle headquarters as a Rocket subsidiary. Redfin’s longtime CEO Glenn Kelman stepped down in January to join the venture firm Greylock as an executive in residence.

Rocket CEO Varun Krishna had been running Redfin since the exit of Kelman, who led the company for more than 20 years and was “one of the industry’s most charismatic and memorable figures,” Real Estate News noted.
In a release announcing Sanfilippo’s hiring, Krishna said that the company’s new leader has spent his career making “complex products work better for enormous audiences.”

“I worked with Alessio at Intuit and saw firsthand how he combines deep analytical thinking with a real instinct for the consumer,” Krishna added. Sanfilippo’s past roles include leadership positions at SAP, goSeek and Hotwire.
Sanfilippo said he has used Redfin for multiple home purchases, adding that the platform “has always helped make an intimidating process easier to understand.”
The company last week joined Zillow in settling an antitrust case with the Federal Trade Commission and five states, just as a trial was set to begin.

The proposed settlement includes an agreement to undo part of a $100 million partnership that the government said effectively paid Redfin to stop competing in apartment rental advertising. The company will now be required to relaunch its apartment advertising operation within six months.

articles.title: What if Rivian spawned an e-bike? We test rode the new two-wheeler from the EV maker’s Also spinoff
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: I pulled a classic Seattle move while test riding an e-bike from Rivian spinout Also last week. It was straight out of the sketch comedy series “Almost Live” and the Ballard Driving Academy : I left my turn signal on.
A turn signal is about the lowest tech feature on the TM-B e-bike (Transcendent Mobility Bike), a Class 3 software-defined machine built around what Also calls its “Dream Ride” system.

The bike feels more like an EV than any two-wheeled commuter I’ve ever ridden. From the digital control portal to the immediate acceleration and regenerative braking, the TM-B is designed to treat hardware as software — relying on a pedal-by-wire powertrain.

While an enclosed belt drive delivers power from the central electric motor to the rear wheel, there is no mechanical chain or physical link connecting your pedals to the drivetrain. Instead, your pedaling acts as a digital controller, telling the motor software how much power to send to the back wheel while generating synthetic gear resistance under your feet.

Also is running a pop-up station at outdoor retailer Evo’s flagship store in Wallingford, where riders can book test spins through the end of the year. Seattle is one of 10 initial launch markets nationwide, giving commuters a chance to put the bike through its paces.

The local pop-up isn’t just a coincidence; it sits directly across from Also’s new office location on Northlake Way. The Palo Alto, Calif.-based company, spun out of EV maker Rivian with a $1 billion valuation, is tapping into Seattle tech and retail talent with a commercial outpost and future retail hub run by REI vet Ben Steele.
Amy Hattemer , Also’s Seattle market manager, walked me through how the TM-B works and what powers it before I set off on a ride through the neighborhood and along the Burke-Gilman Trail.
Here’s a quick look at the core specs for the high-tech bike:

Beyond performance, security is where the bike’s EV heritage really shines through software. The TM-B is built around an integrated digital locking system that disables the entire vehicle at the push of a button — locking down the motor drivetrain, top frame release, and battery compartment, while electronically immobilizing the rear wheel to prevent someone from rolling it away.

When the accompanying mobile app launches, riders will be able to unlock the bike hands-free via smartphone proximity Bluetooth, program custom PIN codes, or use NFC cards. The app will also enable full GPS location tracking, real-time tamper alerts, and digital family key sharing — turning what would normally be a target for bike thieves into a bricked, trackable piece of hardware if left unattended on a city street.

For my ride, I left Evo and took off into Wallingford headed for the University District. The off-the-line power is immediately noticeable and practically dumped me off the seat when I first engaged the thumb throttle.

Thanks to 180 Nm of torque available instantly at the rear wheel — roughly double the pulling power of top-tier cargo bikes — pressing the throttle gets you moving quickly without pedaling. Hattemer called this capability a key safety feature for clearing intersections ahead of right-turning cars.
“It is very powerful,” Hattemer said. “It’s kind of like Mario Kart real life hitting a mushroom, which is pretty great.”

I put the motor to the test by taking the steepest routes I could find, powering up hills in Wallingford before cutting over toward Gas Works Park to zip to the top of the grassy mound. Hattemer noted that in high assist modes, the software flattens out steep inclines so “it will just feel like you were still flat,” and the TM-B delivered on that promise.
Cruising downhill with a combination of pedal assist and throttle, I topped out at 28 mph of exhilarating speed. The regen braking did a nice job of slowing everything down.

Beyond the speed and torque, what sets the TM-B apart from other e-bikes is how tightly controlled that power is through software. Unlike older e-bikes where riders could clip a wire or dig into settings menus to bypass factory governors, Also’s Class 3 limit of 28 mph is hard-coded into the vehicle’s firmware. The company is also planning over-the-air updates that will introduce parental control modes — allowing owners to cap top speeds at 15 mph for younger family members or trail riding.

Back at the test station, Hattemer demonstrated how the bike’s modularity works off the road . Pushing a single eject button releases the top frame, allowing riders to swap between a solo commuter setup, a bench seat, or a heavy-duty cargo rack in about three seconds . Because each frame is digitally serialized to the owner’s account , a single bike body can easily be shared across family members of vastly different heights by swapping top frames and adjusting the seat post .

“I am barely 5-foot-4, and my husband is 6-foot-2, and so we can actually share a bike,” Hattemer said. “So I could have a small top frame, and you could have a large one. So multiple people can use this bike.”
Stripping off the top frame and battery also sheds roughly 25 pounds from the 80-pound bike — a huge practical touch for anyone trying to hoist a heavy commuter onto a standard car rack.

For a city built on steep hills and unpredictable weather, the TM-B makes a compelling case for the future of urban commuting. It isn’t just a high-end e-bike; it’s a fully software-defined vehicle platform — and a sign that Rivian’s automotive DNA has successfully made the jump to two wheels.

articles.title: Rivian spinout Also lands in Seattle, with REI vet leading micromobility startup’s new office and retail hub
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Also , a fast-growing electric micromobility startup born out of Rivian in Silicon Valley, has quietly pulled into Seattle and planted a flag at the epicenter of the city’s bike culture with an office on the north end of Lake Union.

The 17,459-square-foot space at 1300 N. Northlake Way — which previously housed military-grade autonomous vehicle startup Overland AI — is situated directly along the Burke-Gilman Trail at the busy intersection of the Fremont and Wallingford neighborhoods. The headquarters for Brooks Running and the flagship store for outdoor retailer Evo are right across the street.

Ben Steele , Also’s chief commercial officer, is heading up the office. A nine-year veteran of REI, he was attracted to Also’s mission-based vision for the future of micromobility. He’s been tasked with building out the startup’s business operations, marketing, and customer functions from scratch.
First he had to find a dynamic office space. He called the location the hottest spot in the No. 1 bike commuting city in America.

“If you do the heat map in Strava for bike commuting, that is the white-hot spot,” Steele told GeekWire during a tour of the office. “When we said where do we want to be, we want to be where our customers are, where they’re working, where they’re living, where they’re shopping. And we want to be where bike commuters are. And this is that hot spot.”

Founded inside electric vehicle maker Rivian more than three years ago as a special projects group, Palo Alto, Calif.-based Also officially spun out as an independent company in March 2025. The startup is focused on developing software-defined micromobility solutions designed to replace car trips and last-mile commercial delivery, backed by partnerships with Amazon and DoorDash.

Also was co-founded by Rivian founder and CEO RJ Scaringe alongside Chris Yu, Rivian’s former vice president of future programs, who serves as Also’s president. The startup has already commanded major investor backing, achieving a $1 billion unicorn valuation following its spinout to fund vehicle development and scale its commercial operations.

The Seattle space officially opened in April and is currently home to 38 employees, with capacity to grow to around 60 on a second floor featuring sweeping views of Lake Union and the downtown skyline.

Also employs roughly 350 people globally across Palo Alto, Seattle, and a new commercial team in Ghent, Belgium. The hybrid Seattle office requires employees in three days a week — though Steele notes cross-functional visits regularly push daily headcount past 50. The company has drawn talent from Seattle-area giants like REI, Brooks, Rad Power Bikes, Sonos, and Amazon.
Steele pointed to the city’s unique intersection of cycling culture, software technology, and deep consumer retail roots as the primary draw for building a major presence outside Silicon Valley .

“If you think about retail and commercial talent, innovative companies like Nordstrom and Amazon and Starbucks and yes, REI, the talent pool that we have to draw from for this part of the business, this is really the sweet spot to do it,” Steele said.

On the ground floor of the building, Also plans to build out its very first dedicated retail store and customer service bay, complete with space for a co-working or food and beverage partner. Steele called the layout a deliberate move to keep the commercial team grounded in real-world rider interactions.

“The theory is, we want our team really living that experience with our customers,” Steele said . “To have our retail and our office together really means we’re not theorizing about what does that experience look like with our customers. We’re living it every day .”

In the meantime, local riders can try Also’s flagship e-bike, the TM-B , across the street through a pop-up at Evo. Seattle is one of 10 initial U.S. markets where mobile sales teams are conducting test spins out of dedicated vans, coffee shops, and partner locations like Evo and Rivian spaces. Nationwide, the company has already surpassed 10,000 test rides for the high-tech bike, which starts at $3,500.

Beyond personal e-bikes, Also is setting its sights on transforming commercial delivery — a push anchored by a high-profile multi-year collaboration with Amazon, headquartered just across the lake in South Lake Union.

The partnership, announced last fall , centers on a customized pedal-assist e-cargo quad (the TM-Q) designed to navigate dense city centers and operate within dedicated bike lanes. Also plans to roll out prototype units with Amazon in two cities later this year before broader expansion in 2027.

“If you think about a city like Paris, where they’ve closed a lot of Paris down to cars, you can use a vehicle like that to get into the city,” Steele said, pointing out that the quad leverages automotive-grade technology to carry heavy delivery loads up steep hills without the high maintenance of traditional bike chains and derailleurs .

The company is also collaborating with DoorDash to test autonomous last-mile delivery using smaller form-factor vehicles capable of traveling up to 30 mph on streets, hopping curbs, and navigating sidewalks directly to a customer’s front door .

Also enters the market as Seattle’s e-bike landscape undergoes a major shift. The city was once ground zero for breakout success Rad Power Bikes, which helped pioneer consumer e-bikes before suffering a steep post-pandemic downturn that culminated in a Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing and an asset sale early this year.

Steele, who watched Rad’s trajectory from his time leading retail operations at REI, noted that Also is taking explicit notes from the broader e-bike industry’s past missteps. Rather than treating their machines like standard bicycles with added batteries, Also is focusing heavily on custom, automotive-grade hardware and software-defined integration — while staying intentionally lean on retail overhead.
“Building the best e-bike is not our mission,” Steele said. “Building the future of micromobility is our mission. And the first thing we’re building is the best e-bike.”

That philosophy directly shapes how Also plans to roll out its physical footprint. With customer orders now converting and initial Launch Edition bikes shipping over the coming weeks, Steele says the startup is taking an adaptable approach rather than rushing to sign leases on traditional retail store networks.
In addition to fixed hubs like the North Lake Union location, Also is launching a national “test spin tour” using mobile vans to bring 10 bikes and dedicated staff to 20 cities across six weeks.

“I don’t want to be beholden to a single model,” Steele said of the expansion plans. “The thing I wanted to not do is say let’s go build 10 stores and then see if that’s right. Long-term vision is to be really adaptable and really agile with how we do it, and to have what’s the right solution in each market versus a single model that we try to drop in everywhere.”
For Steele, bringing Also to Seattle isn’t just about opening an outpost or testing hardware — it’s about actively shaping the daily routine of local commuters along the lake.
“We want this to be a part of that vibrancy of the neighborhood, not just a place you go by,” Steele said.

That civic integration hits close to home for Steele, who lives near the University of Washington and instead of sitting in his car on Montlake, commutes down the Burke-Gilman Trail on an Also e-bike every morning.
“I arrive at work less stressed out on the Burke-Gilman Trail,” Steele said . “I’m living the product benefit every day. It’s pretty awesome .”

articles.title: Link Ends Earlier, Starts Later
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: Several comments have raised concerns that the August 29th service change shortened Link’s service day, so that it now ends earlier and starts later. This interacts with the launch of ST Express “Night Ride” routes between midnight and 4am. These theoretically can replace Link trips. But the ST Express routes bypass several high-ridership Seattle Link stations. This can force trips that were on Link in the midnight hour or 11 pm hour or 4 am hour to an ST Express or Metro route, turn a 1-seat ride into a 2-seat ride, and the bus routes are less frequent than Link was.

I wanted to know, did the spans really change on August 29? What is the current situation on weekdays, Saturdays, and Sundays? What kinds of trips at what hours are newly 2-seat rides? Where is the best place to live to have the earliest or latest Link service? Which can you go to on those lucky runs?

I looked at the new 1 Line and 2 Line schedules to quantify the current situation and changes. To reach these pages from Sound Transit’s website, use the schedule form on the home page to get to the interactive charts. To get a PDF of the schedule, go to the bottom of the page and press the “Full Schedule PDF” button.
I tried to make a consolidated list that would organize the first/last runs in different areas and days. But it was an insanely difficult job, and after a few hours I gave up.
So instead we’re going to crowdsource the issue.

How has Link’s span changed since August 29th? Has this affected your trips? Or do you see other people’s trips that are affected? Can you glean more from the schedules than I can? Can you figure out the right questions to ask AI to figure it out? (If you do, please disclose AI’s role in the result.)

Some of these impacts have already come up in recent articles’ comments, but this article is a place to consolidate them all together so we can see the total impact. And it will be a reference in the future when people have a question, so that they can find it all in one easy-to-find place.

The problem I had with the interactive schedule pages was I had to keep scrolling four directions to get at the first or last full run and short run, and when that would get you to Westlake or SeaTac or the final terminus. I had to keep going up to the date switcher. I kept finding mistake after mistake in my results, so I had to go back and reconfirm them, or compare weekday to Saturday again, and make sure I hadn’t jumped back to a date before the service change. Reading the PDFs online was a lot of up-and-down scrolling with similar printing. Printing the PDFs to get a wider-area view at once would take 34 pages per line. Maybe ST has a printed schedule book with them but I’d have to go search for a copy. I didn’t want to publish a list with mistakes that would waste everybody’s time.
Maybe if different people address small parts of the issue individually, we can get those facts more accurately and a better idea of the whole.

ST in the future wants to shorten Link’s span further, or have more single-track reductions, or more weekend closures of segments, to increase the time available for maintenance. We desperately want ST to increase maintenance because Link’s reliability is far below peer cities’ networks. This causes passengers to get stuck en route, be late for appointments, or drive to critical appointments to avoid the risk that Link will hiccup that day. It also snares visitors and gives them a negative impression of Seattle and Seattle’s transit. So we really want maintenance to be increased to make Link more reliable.

At the same time we need Link’s late-night and early-morning service. If ST Express night owls bypass several Seattle stations in the shoulder hours Link used to provide, then it’s not an adequate substitute. ST says Metro has night owl buses in all those areas (7, 36, 49, 67, 70). But those night runs are funded by Seattle’s transit levy, and will go away if voters don’t renew the levy this November. Metro stopped funding Seattle night owls in the 2014 recession. Also, the bus routes are half-hourly or hourly, as opposed to Link’s 15 minutes. If you switch to say the 49+597 or 36+597 to workaround the loss of Link, you may be waiting 30+30 minutes or a full hour.

This affects people coming home from bars, staff working at bars, people who start or end a night shift, people going to the airport for an early-morning flight, and people coming from an evening flight that was delayed and didn’t land until midnight or later, and airport workers with early-morning shifts.

So what are the actual problems now? Did Link’s span decrease August 29th? What kinds of trips, where, and when are affected? If in the future ST ends Link even earlier at 10pm or 9 pm every day or on monthly maintenance days or two-week maintenance periods, how big a deal would that be? How would we cope with it? What should we tell Sound Transit and our politicians about all this?

articles.title: Announcing Special Guests for Our CityNerd Talk, Plus a Call for Volunteers
articles.author: Diego Batres
paras: We are looking for volunteers to help handle check-in and act as ushers. Volunteers will receive free entry to the event in return for arriving early to help set up. If you are interested in volunteering, email Diego@theurbanist.org .

Claudia Balducci has served on the King County Council since 2016 and on the Sound Transit Board of Directors since 2010. Before joining county council, she was a Bellevue City Councilmember and Mayor. She has been a key leader on the Sound Transit board, including a long run as Chair of the System Expansion Committee that just ended earlier this year. She has also led on housing, establishing and co-leading the Regional Affordable Housing Taskforce and chairing the King County Affordable Housing Committee. articles.title: Winter Rollback of Pike Place Market Pedestrian Pilot Moves Forward
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Last week, the Pike Place Market Historical Commission gave its unanimous approval to planned adjustments around vehicle access through Seattle's iconic market. Set to be in effect from October through next March, the adjustments represent the newest phase of a pedestrian pilot program that has been in effect for nearly 18 months, but have been lambasted as a retreat on an issue that has widespread city support – restricting unnecessary car traffic through the market.

Under the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) plan , the main corridor along Pike Place will only experience "soft closures" on Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays, with the hours vehicles are restricted slightly tightened up to 11am to 4pm. Soft closures mean access is restricted to delivery vehicles, ADA access for disabled patrons, and market vendors.

Apart from major event days when the street will fully close with barricades, through car traffic will be unrestricted along the street with "street closed" signage switched to signage telling drivers to yield to pedestrians.

Pointing to a SDOT survey conducted earlier this year showing 98% support for maintaining vehicle barriers through the Market, a sizable contingent of Seattle urbanists have lamented the move as a backslide that isn't in alignment with the broader city's desires for a more pedestrian-oriented Pike Place. But many Market vendors have argued that they weren't included in the initial launch of the pedestrian pilot in April of 2025, a move made in response to a utility repair project along Stewart Street.

"There are a lot of strong feelings and ideas that we heard from a lot of different people. So, I think ideas are as diverse and dynamic as the number of businesses in the market and all the people who also use this street," Radcliffe Dacanay, the SDOT project manager who has been tasked with leading this work at Pike Place, told commissioners. "There were some increased sales [that] some vendors expressed, but not all vendors experienced increased sales. So, that data is varied. Some sales improved, some vendors [it did] not. But also, just this sense of the Market as a place to come to, and not just an errand space."

The historic commission does get final buy-off on changes of either use or design within the seven-acre historic district. But SDOT's recommendation for the pilot's next phase came about after months of discussions with Market power players, including the commission's chair Jon Cracolici, Alex Hudson from Mayor Katie Wilson's office, members of the Pike Place Merchant's Association (rebooted just this year after being defunct for years), and representatives for the Pike Place Public Development Authority (PDA) which directly maintains operations along the street.

During the meeting, PDA Chief Operating Officer Katie Trent framed the winter access plan as an improvement over last winter, because the PDA had not been enforcing vehicle access restrictions on any weekdays through the Market's quieter months. Trent's comments gloss over the change in signage that will fairly explicitly encourage drivers to head down Pike Place
Trent also provided a new counterpoint to the positive sales data seen at the market in 2025, when it comes to year-over-year (YOY) data for the first half of 2026.

Between January and June, visits to the Market from local residents coming less than 30 miles declined by 11% compared to 2025, a trend that only started to reverse itself in July, with a 1% YOY increase seen in that month. Over those six months, total sales did continue to increase at the Market, but growth slowed from 7% in 2025 to 4.7% this year. Grocery sales took at 4.5% hit during the second quarter, a fact that can likely be traced to the shift in visitor trends during the FIFA Men's World Cup.

"There's all kinds of things that can contribute to what goes on with visitation and sales data, but the street has been an element in there," Trent said. "We have vendors coming to us and saying, 'I'm losing customers because of this, especially in the offseason. Why is the street closed?' That's impactful to what we want to promote as the operator."

The shift toward seasonal operations was bolstered by a study conducted by the University of Washington's Urban Freight Lab – a study that makes some leaps on the way to getting to its conclusions, based on the fact that fewer people visit the Market in the winter overall than in the summer. But it became clear during Wednesday's meeting that SDOT and the PDA had come together to land on a threshold of Market visitation to justify the new schedule: 3,300 Market visitors per hour, or around 55 people passing through the street every minute.
During the summer months, that threshold has been easily met, but in the slower months it has not, according to PDA data from 2025.

Despite presenting the methodology behind the proposal, some merchants and commenters – including members of the advocacy nonprofit group Friends of the Market – wanted to drop soft closures on Fridays. That point of contention pushed this proposal toward looking more like a compromise. It's important to note that the PDA is also empowered to restrict vehicle access if foot traffic is more than expected – and in turn, to cancel soft closures early if the Market is a ghost town on a Friday in February.

"I support this plan. I thought it was very thoughtfully put together. As a vendor, I felt included in the process, both by Urban Freight Lab and the PDA and the working group. I really appreciate what SDOT did in hearing our needs and continues to," Bite Society owner Lendy Hensley said. "I didn't get everything I wanted in this. I suspect no one did, and sometimes I think that is the best kind of agreement. I hope the process continues, as somebody who's looking at Fridays and thinking maybe not that. So I'm hoping for continued conversation as we get to see what these winter months actually look like with this framework in mind."
Plenty of speakers at last week's meeting did provide a voice for the idea of keeping the pedestrian pilot in effect seven days a week.

"I think the thing that I was very disappointed in when I moved to the Market is how uncomfortable it was to shop at the Market and to walk down the streets and try to find my way through the sidewalks," resident Larry Goetz said. "I really appreciate what SDOT did in closing the traffic for the last year and a half, I think it has worked beautifully, especially for the World Cup games. I think it really works. I would like to see it continue."

What happens this winter will likely only set the stage for the Market's next new normal, with SDOT set to return to the commission in January for a proposal for what next summer looks like at Pike Place, without a World Cup to plan around. But at some point, the pilot will need to draw to a close, shifting to a more permanent program.

"I hope that we don't do this every six months," commissioner Mark Childs said ahead of Wednesday's vote. "That this actually builds to something that can last for a period of time, and that there's certainty that people can build around."

articles.title: CHS Pics | ‘ROUND AND ROUND THEY GO’ — Tilted Thunder Roller Derby battles on 15th Ave E
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: There was a taped-out oval on the floor of the Quality Flea Center on 15th Ave E this weekend and it didn’t get there by accident.
Taylor Sloan , who runs the bar at The Hopvine across the street, spent part of her week free-handing a flat track onto the flea market’s concrete floor, no measuring tape required.
“I’ve taped out a million tracks at this point,” Sloan said. “I use upholstery foam and gaffer tape for the pole covers, because it’s supposed to be like a fun, DIY, punk rock sort of thing.”

Sloan has been skating with Tilted Thunder Roller Derby for 17 years. Normally, that means suiting up on the league’s regular turf: a 6,000-square-foot wooden track the team builds from scratch at the fairgrounds in Monroe, home to a growing in popularity event –polished, bleacher-seated, and fiercely competitive. But this weekend at the Quality Flea Center was something else entirely with a stripped-down expo bout, played bank track rules on the flat surface with skaters squaring off against each other for the fun of it.
Sloan also tends bar at the Flea Center whenever it hosts markets and the derby-slash-rock-show idea had been kicking around in her head for a while.
“I wanted to do a crazy, fun, old-school style derby slash rock show, and that’s what this is,” she said. “It’s just an expo bout, just a demo game.”

The music lineup came together the way a lot of good DIY bills do, through a cold DM. Sloan found the band Good Grief on social media and asked them to come play a roller derby show. “They said hell yes,” she said. Daniel Cadaver , a band that’s also played the area, rounds out the bill.

Money-wise, it all came down to ticket sales. “We’ll split with the bands once the cost of the event is covered,” Sloan explained. Unlike Tilted Thunder’s Monroe productions, which come with the overhead of a full fairground buildout, the Quality Flea Center version keeps costs down to the essentials: alcohol insurance, security, and the venue itself. “This is a show,” Sloan said. “I love being very competitive [at the big track], but it’s also fun to take time out of your life to just do something crazy and fun, something that reminds you of another time.”

For anyone on Capitol Hill who’s never seen a bout, Sloan’s pitch is simple: Go find your local league, because there almost certainly is one. Roller derby’s modern era, she said, was built from the ground up by women in the early 2000s, and leagues like Tilted Thunder have been sustaining it ever since on their own time and their own dime. ”
We continue to put all of our time, money, effort, blood, sweat, tears, partners, work, everything, into this sport because it’s just so fun,” Sloan said.
What keeps her coming back, she said, is what makes derby different from a lot of other sports. There’s a role for every body type, and nobody gets left out.
“Every single person, at every single body type, has a purpose and a strength and is celebrated,” Sloan said. “There is no one that is left out or shamed.”
For now, most of the Tilted Thunder action takes places in Monroe but keep your eyes peeled for another visit to the Hill. Learn more at tiltedthunder.org .

articles.title: Plan for higher caps in Broadway Business Improvement Area moves forward
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Watch video of the committee approval here

With the Seattle City Council still in the midst of its summer legislative recess, the city’s lawmakers will have an important piece of Capitol Hill business to addend to when they return to chambers.

Legislation modernizing the assessment structure for the Broadway Business Improvement Area for the first time in over two decades to fund neighborhood clean-up, public safety, and promotion initaitives is planned to come in front of the full council September 15th.

A council committee approved the legislation earlier this month. CHS examined the proposal here. The plan will raise the district’s maximum annual rate from $3,500 to $5,000, expanding its current approximate $200,000 a year budget before adding a recurring $200 annual increase starting in 2032.

During the session, the BBIA’s longtime administrator Egan Orion told the council’s Human Services, Labor, and Economic Development Committee chair Alexis Mercedes Rinck that the change is much needed — and could be the next step in an even more impactful upgrade to the neighborhood clean-up and promotion organization’s finances.

“The costs for garbage pickup and graffiti abatement have increased with inflation, and yet our assessments, especially from our max payers, have remained relatively flat,” Orion told the committee. “So this creates a more equitable assessment for all and it allows the BIA to continue at current service levels plus add back promotion, beautification budgets, event sponsorship, and more.”

Orion said more may be needed and that the BBIA and officials are exploring “a property-based model or establishing a brand-new BIA and sunsetting this particular model”, as property-based assessments “are more sustainable than B&O-based assessments.”

The Broadway BIA was established decades ago as a business-tenant levy. The assessment formula is levied directly on the commercial tenants and operators within the BIA boundary. The typical small-to-midsize business currently pays between $400 and $1,500 annually, depending on its size and reported gross revenue.

A proposed Pike/Pine BIA in the works for years would be property-based. Its formation would give the neighborhood three. The 15th Ave E BIA provides similar services from assessments collected along a core stretch of Capitol Hill’s 15th Ave E.
It is unclear at this point if officials would have the stomach for trying to include the current Broadway BIA zone in a larger IA including Pike/Pine.

A decade ago, the Capitol Hill Chamber of Commerce backed down after a years-long fight against smaller Capitol Hill property owners over a planned expansion of the 1986-born Broadway BIA that would have grown the area to cover most of the Hill including the neighborhoods around Summit/Bellevue, Olive and Denny, Pike/Pine, 12th Ave, 15th Ave, and 19th Ave. The expended energy and flagging membership contributed to the chamber’s shutdown months later .
Some of Broadway’s largest voices are supporting the currently proposed growth for the BIA.

Under the legislation headed for final approval by the full council in September, anchor institutions like Seattle Central College and neighborhood bank branches would become standard maximum-rate payers to reinforce basic maintenance services managed by the BIA across more than 150 businesses along the Broadway commercial corridor.

“We have underpaid for 25 years, and we are probably the largest footprint in the Broadway neighborhood association,” a Seattle Central official said before the August committee vote. “We find it to be absolutely equitable for us to have our limit increased… the value that we receive is massive.”

Committee member, council president, and District 3 representative Joy Hollingsworth did not address the potential larger changes around the Broadway BIA surfaced by Orion but did emphasize the organization’s focus beyond Pike/Pine.

“I think oftentimes North Broadway, the area that you cover, kind of gets left out of the mix,” Hollingsworth said, “because we get so focused on Pike/Pine corridor that we forget that there’s a large part of Capitol Hill that extends to North Broadway and then the area that the BIA covers.”
For now, the Broadway BIA as it stands from E Pike to E Roy is set for a financial boost and any larger changes are being debated outside of City Hall.

articles.title: Damage limited as Seattle Fire battles early morning blaze in historic E Madison apartment building
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Firefighters battled an early morning fire in a historic E Madison apartment building Monday.

Seattle Fire was called to the 1912-era Olympian Apartments in the 1600 block of E Madison just after 5:15 AM to reports of flames coming from a lower floor of the six-story structure and its distinctive terra cotta cladding.
Crews reported the fire under control about 15 minutes later but were working to remove smoke from the upper floors of the building.
SFD said that crews were able to contain the blaze before it damaged any additional areas of the building.
The cause of the fire is under investigation.
According to the city’s database of historic properties, the “Beaux Arts – Neoclassical”-style building is worthy of landmarks status but not yet under protection of the ordinance.

articles.title: District says negotiations stall over teacher demand for 6% raise on top of state-funded cost-of-living adjustments
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Superintendent Ben Shuldiner said contract negotiations for a new teachers contract stalled in a message to student families over the weekend.

Negotiations between Seattle Public Schools and the Seattle Education Association were unable to move forward, prompting the district to request a mediator from the Public Employment Relations Commission , Shuldiner said in the Sunday update.

Shuldiner said the district sought mediation after rejecting the union’s latest counterproposal as regressive bargaining, arguing the new submission added millions of dollars in costs to earlier demands.
The district’s contract package offers educators an 8.8% salary increase over three years with no furlough days, tied to state cost-of-living adjustments.

Additional provisions include adding six psychologists, assigning a full-time social worker or counselor to schools with more than 350 students, and restructuring special education models to keep students in neighborhood schools with increased behavioral support.
The proposal also features district-funded VEBA health accounts, reduced monthly staff meetings, and an additional paid training day for more than 1,500 paraprofessionals and office staff.

The 8.8% pay raise over three years would pass through projected state-funded cost-of-living adjustments with no local increase. In contrast, the Seattle Education Association is proposing the same state inflation adjustment plus an additional 6.0% wage increase over three years, alongside targeted bumps for paraprofessionals and office staff.

CHS reported last week as the union authorized a strike as union leaders say that members are seeking an agreement focused on shifting resources to the classroom, strengthening special education supports, along with “respectful pay,” and “easing pressurization on educators” with smaller class sizes.
SEA represents 6,000 teachers, paraeducators, counselors, and support staff.

Seattle Public Schools is facing a chronic structural budget deficit, operating with an annual general fund budget of roughly $1.35 billion while managing annual shortfalls in the $90 million to $130 million range. The state allocates school funding primarily on a per-pupil model. With its enrollment dropping, SPS loses tens of millions annually in state basic education funding. Meanwhile, federal pandemic relief funds have fully expired.
The median and average salary for Seattle Public Schools teachers sits at approximately $117,000 per year.
In its latest public update Friday, SEA said its members were preparing over the weekend with picket sign making and picket practice at Judkins Park.
The dispute comes four years after the union took the rare step of launching a strike in pounding out a contract with the district in 2022 with wins on special education and salaries.
A state mediator has been assigned to help the parties bridge remaining divides before the school year begins. The first day of classes in Seattle is scheduled for Wednesday.

articles.title: More labor disputes: State workers hold walkout over contract, working conditions
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: There are more ripples of labor unrest around Seattle. Thousands of Washington public employees are staging a statewide walkout across more than 100 worksites Monday, demanding higher wages and better working conditions.
Nearby walkout sites include the Washington State Department of Social and Health Services office on E Cherry and the University of Washington .

Representing 52,000 state workers, the Washington Federation of State Employees said in its announcement that uncompetitive compensation and severe understaffing are eroding essential public services, higher education, and healthcare. Union leaders criticized state negotiators for failing to match inflation, noting Washington spent a record $537 million on legal liability payouts in fiscal year 2026 alone.
Workers argue that chronic underfunding fuels costly turnover and overreliance on private contractors, urging state leaders to invest directly in front-line staff.

One specific conflict could impact Seattle Central students. The WFSE Community College Coalition are negotiating a contract for workers at 12 community colleges including the Seattle Colleges system.
Like the negotiations currently underway with Seattle Public Schools teachers , the community college sides are tussling over adjusting base pay to keep up with inflation and rising costs of living.

articles.title: Consider Where You Park an E-Bike in South Seattle, Blind and Deafblind Folks Say
paras: "Safety needs to be number one," said Mae Lynn Mullen, a Columbia City resident who is deaf and has visual impairment. "It's come to a point where [multiple] scooters or bikes are turned over at a four-way intersection, and people are just walking over them and around them. I don't accept that. We can do better," said Mullen, signing briskly, about how dangerous it is for her to move about with lax enforcement of improperly parked shared electric vehicles. "People with baby strollers can't get through. It impacts wheelchair users, seniors, and Deafblind people," she said through an American Sign Language (ASL) interpreter.

Mullen's partner, Roger Poulin, who's both deaf and blind and an avid distance walker, described encountering improperly parked Lime electric vehicles around Columbia City, including at an intersection to the neighborhood's light rail station, along South Edmunds Street near PCC, and along the trail through Columbia Park. Poulin said he's been reporting each case he comes across and moving the bikes out of the way for years, "but I'm not seeing any change. I feel like they don't care, and it's frustrating," Poulin said through an interpreter. "I just want to toss the bikes," Poulin said, as he thrust his arms forward.

Poulin and Mullen often frequent neighborhood food haunts. They're among dozens of Deafblind and blind community members who live in, work, or commute through Southeast Seattle to access service hubs, such as the Washington State Department of Services for the Blind (DSB) in Columbia City and The Lighthouse for the Blind in Mount Baker.

Lime's Seattle fleet of 15,000 electric vehicles are found in many neighborhoods, and they were used for 10.5 million trips last year. The vehicles can decrease dependence on car rides because they offer an alternative to short trips, including walking the last leg of a commute after a transit ride. Public complaints about them include the safety of using electric vehicles and improper parking.

The Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) wrote in a statement that "Scooters and bikes should be parked upright in out‑of‑the‑way spots such as bike racks, bike corrals, or near trees and poles close to the curb. Riders need to always leave at least six feet of clear space for people walking." Additionally, SDOT noted "Micromobility should not be parked on sidewalks, at curb ramps, intersections, driveways, bus stops, City of Seattle parks, or in front of building entrances, benches, pay stations, fire hydrants, or waste bins." (Micromobility refers to the use of single-person transportation, such as bikes or scooters, to travel short distances.)

Parker Dawson, Lime's Senior Regional Lead of Government Relations for the Pacific Northwest, wrote in a statement, "Riders found to repeatedly mispark vehicles can face increasing penalties, including fines , suspension and, ultimately, expulsion from the Lime platform."

"Everyone in this community has a story about run-ins with micromobility," said David Miller, an orientation and mobility specialist for the Deafblind community who specializes in training Deafblind people on how to make use of public transportation.

Miller frequently receives requests from the Deafblind community to report misparked Lime e-bikes and e-scooters, since it's often cumbersome for this community to report it themselves. Miller uses the city's Find It, Fix It app. SDOT also has a hotline, 206-684-ROAD (7623) and email address.

According to a statement from Ethan Bergerson, SDOT press secretary, "Bad parking reported in the [city's] Find It, Fix it app is sent to Lime, and then Lime sends one of their workers to move the device." After that, "The city fines Lime and [Lime] pay[s] the City for every violation."

Last year, Lime paid the city $74,500 in fines related to parking obstructions and other compliance issues, separate from its $1.28 million operations permit costs. Bergerson wrote that the fees from Lime pay for "our bike and scooter share program operational costs including staff and building new corrals. A portion of the fees also supports Outdoors for All, which provides free adaptive cycle rentals for people with disabilities." In 2025, Lime received $37.4 million from Seattle rides, according to Post Alley .

In one training session, Miller trained Charles Mendoza, a Deafblind retiree who was a machinist for 38 years. Mendoza practiced how to navigate light rail from Capitol Hill to the Kent Des Moines Station. "People who are sighted have no problem [with Lime vehicles]," Mendoza said through an interpreter, "but for us, it isn't safe because we encounter them and might fall." Mendoza and Poulin have both tripped and fallen because of improperly parked e-vehicles.

Kevin Southworth, who is Deafblind, used to have a career in IT before his vision deteriorated. He commutes to a manufacturing job in Southeast Seattle. He said he's fallen a couple of times because of micromobility devices. He recalled there were two e-bikes parked in a row, and he cleared one, not realizing there was another next to it. He tripped and landed on the vehicle, cutting his chin and mouth. "[Electric vehicles] need to be off to the side or in designated areas," he said through an interpreter, and rubbed his chin.

SDOT has marked corral spaces to park Lime vehicles in a number of areas with high micromobility use. But Alice Klein, DSB orientation and mobility specialist, noted, "A painted line on the sidewalk is not detectable by a cane, and so a person might be traveling, and they might inadvertently walk into a corral with a number of Lime vehicles in it." Klein and Miller attend the SDOT Pedestrian Access Advisory Committee meetings and have been advocating for micromobility corrals with tactile boundaries discernable by a cane. The City installed three of five planned corrals this month to test out the edges of tactile border pads in downtown Seattle. They passed Miller and Klein's standards, and the two are hopeful that more tactile-identifiable corral borders can be installed in high-density transit locations.

Miller said the Deafblind community uses tools to navigate where they are in their commute. They consider the directions of slopes as markers, as well as their cane and a complementary Miniguide, an electronic travel device that uses echolocation and vibrates differently depending on how close the user is to an object. Deafblind commuters count the number of stops on a light rail route. They check in with the bus driver using a card. Electric vehicles, cones used to caution people about a wet or slippery floor, skateboards, tents and other things are obstacles that can impact navigation.

"The margin of error is small," said Miller. "A wrong turn can take you on a path to the Eastside when you wanted to go to Capitol Hill, or can land you on the light rail platform going the opposite direction from where you wanted to go, in which case you would be totally lost."
Have something to say about Lime shared vehicles in the city? Take the current Seattle survey on Seattle's bike and scooter share program.
Need to report improperly parked shared electric vehicles?
SDOT Hotline: 206-684-ROAD (7623) or 684-Road@Seattle.gov

articles.title: The Iota at Carrello
articles.author: Meg van Huygen
paras: I will be real with you. I’ve had trouble getting a handle on what Carrello is all about. The sister restaurant to fabulous Altura opened across the street in 2022, and I know the intended bent is Italian-ish, and that chef Nathan Lockwood is a big meat guy who’s finicky about sourcing and breaks down whole animals himself. But what is the concept? I love ending up at Carrello, but the memory of the meal is always slippery. Meaty pasta and beautiful cocktails, no complaints—it’s all a savory, flavory blur. Like, a carrello is a cart. Great, love carts, use them all the time. What exactly is in this cart? There are two things I do always remember about lovely Carrello. One is the dreamy eastern-facing patio and adjacent curated chef’s garden, with all the kaboingy telephone-cord squash tendrils climbing up the fence. And one’s the Iota.

A new friend recently suggested we hit Carrello to try their happy hour menu in its entirety, and I don’t really need to know what kind of cart we’re getting in before accepting this prompt. This is my kind of lady right here. What I didn’t realize is that Carrello’s doing a thing called Abbinamento (Italian for “coupling”) where you can get mini versions of each HH drink and each dish, as a pairing, for $79 total. We let all six drink/snack sets flow all over us, and while it was all a tone poem in hedonism, there were two big standouts. The lamb ribs and peppers are dressed lightly with mint, chili, and toasted rice powder that added a tiny crunch. A mouse stepping on a leaf. You get three small ribs in the mini HH version, stacked like Jenga blocks, with the roasted baby peppers tumbling around them, glistening and winking at you in the candlelight. The rendered lamb fat is so grassy and herby and flavorful, it’s like an umami compound butter all by itself. My word.

And that Iota, which is called the Greek Melon Punch on the HH menu; on the full cocktail list, we learn its true name. Bar director Derek Danley explains that this is a cover of a clarified milk punch. He uses cucumber-infused gin with Acqua di Cedro citrus liqueur, freshly juiced cantaloupe, and Fino sherry infused with four different types of mint from the chef’s garden, along with lemon juice and “our house ferment.” Your what? “Well,” he says, “our kitchen makes this by mixing a ton of seasonal veggies like carrots, celery, onions, and garlic, as well as seasonal stuff like fennel, lovage, radish.” He keeps some of the strained liquid behind the bar to add tang and richness to his cocktails. So Danley takes some that active, funky garden juice, adds all the cocktail’s ingredients to it except the Greek yogurt and milk, and then pours this boozy potion into the dairy mix. “I let that sit for about 30 minutes and then filter everything,” he says. “It’s a process that usually takes about two days to fully filter, but it leaves the cocktail looking crystal clear, while giving it an incredibly luxurious, velvet texture.”

The beverage itself is the palest yellow, made of opalescent sunlight. Not sure why it took society this long to figure out that cantaloupe is the ideal melon for cocktails, not honeydew, but I’m thrilled to live in this era. The aroma of its cousin, the cucumber, hangs in the air over the drink like an enchanted mist, and it’s all imbued with a barely-there minty, milky, citrusy tang. The garden brine is fucking heavenly. With apologies to my nephews, the word that comes to mind is dank . I want to stick my face in the forbidden, ever-changing pickle jar. Put a crazy straw in there that spells out my name. Okay. Now I see. The actual point of Carrello is the garden. This is, I’ve decided, a garden restaurant where they serve various rustic Italian dishes that are accented by the dreamy onsite urban food garden .

After we finish the six-course Abbinamento mini-food/mini-cocktail pairing experience, I order a grown-up Iota for dessert. I want to drink it some more. For this one, Danley serves the drink in a poco grande glass over a custom ice cube, embossed on which seems to be the screensaver maze from my family’s mid-’90s IBM 386. My friend leans in and reveals that she knew I’d love this cocktail and it’s the specific reason she brought me here. I feel known.
I think this is gonna work out. We just get each other now—my new pal and Carrello both.

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, August 31–September 6
articles.author: Julianne Bell, Dylan Bueche, Nathalie Graham, Amanda Manitach, Megan Seling, and Nico Swenson
paras: (PERFORMANCE) Jane Don’t is Seattle’s latest star to compete on RuPaul’s Drag Race . If you’ve seen her locally, you already know she was poised to do well. Her drag style uses vintage aesthetics in contemporary ways, combining her knowledge of queer history, fashion references, and her own innovative sewing skills. With a fully glamorous mug, she delivers high-camp performances full of witty pop-culture and classic diva references. Her talents especially come out when she’s handed a microphone to show off her seemingly effortless grasp on comedy. On the show, that skill in particular led her to high praise from comedy giants such as special guest judges Sarah Sherman and Atsuko Okatsuka. If you haven’t gathered yet, she absolutely crushed it, right up until a shocking elimination in the top 5 of Season 18. She made a record-smashing run of high placements, and claimed the title of Miss Congeniality during the finale. Jane Don’t truly made Seattle proud, and proved to the world she is one of the best in the business. She will kick off her extensive Don’t Does America tour in her hometown. ( Emerald City Comedy Club, 7:30, 21+ ) NICO SWENSON
Get yourself some Maui Wowie and snacks and watch 9 to 5

(FILM) Somehow, at the ripe age of 35, I saw 9 to 5 for the first time earlier this year (I know, I know) and couldn’t believe how sharp, funny, joyful, and subversive it was, even today. I have a half-baked conspiracy theory that the streamers bury it on purpose, because what do you mean there’s a scene where Dolly Parton, Jane Fonda, and Lily Tomlin all get zooted on Maui Wowie and indulge in elaborate fantasies of murdering their boss? (Dream blunt rotation for real.) Or that there’s a part where they’re all dressed up in medieval princess costumes ? Not to mention the fact that the film does a much better job of tackling issues like female solidarity, sexual harassment, and sexism in the workplace than a lot of current-day media does, but I digress. In honor of Dolly, I propose this weeknight plan: Pick up some Maui Wowie in your preferred form at your friendly local dispensary, swing by the grocery store for some buttery microwave popcorn and Dolly Parton’s original whipped cheesecake or chocolate pie , and press play on this delightful classic, which is streaming for free on Philo . (Normally I’d recommend you rent it from Scarecrow Video , but that might not be feasible right now, for obvious reasons ). Then read Fonda’s touching tribute to Parton . JULIANNE BELL

(MUSIC) Singer-songwriter, mezzo-soprano, and classically trained pianist Tori Amos needs no introduction. The influential feminist musician’s newest album, In Times of Dragons , tells the story of a woman who transforms into a half-human, half-dragon figure and is described as a “metaphorical story about the fight for Democracy over Tyranny, reflecting the current abhorrent non accidental burning down of democracy in real time by the ‘Dictator believing Lizard Demons’ in their usurpation of America.” Recorded at Amos’s home studio in Cornwall, the album invokes spiritual muses like Teresa of Ávila, the Celtic deity Lugh, and the Egyptian goddess Sekhmet. It also includes characters like a gay witch from Brooklyn and the motorcycling “Gasoline Girls” who “kiss girls”—I’m sold. The Baltimore-based artist/producer Bartees Strange will open. ( Chateau Ste. Michelle, 7 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

(VISUAL ART) Becca Fuhrman’s vibrant, color-dense imagery often centers around female protagonists—a celebration of feminine strength, sensuality, and balls. There’s also a thread of the autobiographical peeking out from the nip slips and opulent patterns. In Eat it All , Fuhrman’s first solo Seattle show, the autobiographical punches through as a “rebellious act of survival born from living in the pressure-cooker of beauty culture,” and a protest against the consumerist edict to do anything but grow old. This new body of work is about bodies, our relationship to mortality, and the intensity of being alive. Supple flesh, skulls, a roll of dice, and fallen flowers are traditional vanitas motifs given a fresh spin as they weave throughout paintings and sculptures, like little defiant Easter eggs screaming fuck you to the patriarchy. ( Hometeam Gallery ) AMANDA MANITACH

(MUSIC) With a sound described as “Charli XCX on whippets” and a look modeled on the MySpace-era aesthetic and Y2K bimbo queens, Slayyyter is the bratty, trashy-fabulous diva that the chronically online gays have been waiting for. The “anti-pop star” and former Cookie Monster pajamas girl’s third studio album, WOR$T GIRL IN AMERICA , is a no-skips wonder that sounds like it’s been freshly ripped from a hot pink iPod Nano, inspired by her teen years in St. Louis. The lead single “Beat Up Chanel$” evokes, as the lyrics go, “drunk high school nights in parking lots, hanging at the skate park watching the boys, longing for designer items I couldn’t afford,” while “Brittany Murphy” expresses Slayyyter’s suicidal thoughts and her identification with the late Uptown Girls actress. The Showbox stop on her world tour is an opportunity to see an unstoppable artist at the top of her game—plus, a dollar of each ticket sold will be donated to local LGBTQ+ organizations. ( Showbox, 8 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

(COMMUNITY) The perfect way to spend a late summer evening is to gather at Green Lake at dusk and learn all about Seattle’s local bat species. Bats Northwest is hosting this informational talk. The length of which depends on the weather and the bats. You can bank on it lasting at least 1.5 hours, though. You will leave as a bat expert. The event is free. But it is a BYOC (bring your own chair) event. ( West Green Lake Beach, 7:15 pm ) NATHALIE GRAHAM

(MUSIC) Phew! Another music festival? But it’s September! Isn’t it time to go back to school and drink hot cocoa under a cozy blanket and pretend to care about football? No! There is still summer fun to be had, as exhausted as you may be, because Bumbershoot is taking over the Seattle Center September 5 and 6 with two days of music, comedy, art, wrestling, fashion, and so much more. (Like, literally there is a mermaid???) We know how overwhelming festivals can be, and this year’s Bumbershoot lineup, while smaller than previous iterations, is still loaded with so much good shit. Bikini Kill! De La Soul! Noname! Peaches! So we did your homework for you and wrote up every! single! band! playing over the weekend, as well as all the fun arts and culture and cat stuff. We crammed it all into an exhaustive guide that you can pick up around town, at the festival, and online at TheStranger.com . Sleep is overrated anyway. ( Seattle Center, times vary, all ages ) MEGAN SELING

(FILM) In French New Wave director Jacques Rivette’s delightful 1974 film Céline and Julie Go Boating , magician Céline (Juliet Berto) and librarian Julie (Dominique Labourier) cross paths in a park in Paris and instantly form a playful bond. Soon, the pair stumbles upon a haunted house that replays a murder-mystery melodrama in an incessant loop, and they become entangled in its repetitive narrative. Rivette worked closely with his two stars to create the film, which ranks at #78 on Sight & Sound ’s list of the 100 Greatest Films of All Time. (Fun fact: It partially inspired the 1985 buddy comedy and Madonna vehicle Desperately Seeking Susan .) At 193 minutes long, this movie isn’t for those with short attention spans, but dreamers will definitely fall under its spell and shouldn’t pass up the chance to see it screened at our film Genius Award winner, the Beacon Cinema. (They’ve also got a bunch of other cool stuff scheduled for this month, including Jess Franco’s 1988 Eyes Without a Face remake Faceless , Charlie Kaufman’s debut Synecdoche, New York , and the Bette Davis melodrama The Little Foxes —check it out!) ( Beacon Cinema, 6 pm ) JULIANNE BELL

Esteemed Italian restaurant Mezzanotte’s end-of-the-summer block party is back for the third year in a row! Take a “Georgetown pause” and come check out this all-time lineup of staff, friends, and locals as Mezzanotte’s garden patio sonically transforms to rival even the sounds of passing planes. For the cost of $20 (a Seattle fiver), there are eight bands—Fan Club, Sux, Ononos, Dish Pit, Scott Yoder, Brat, Microfoam, and Understater—and it starts at 4 p.m. and wraps up around dark (take that, Zoo Tunes), so you can be in bed early Sunday night. All ages are welcome, and kids get in free. ( Mezzanotte, 4 pm, all ages ) DYLAN BUECHE

articles.title: Slog AM: War’s on Again, ICE Detains Man with Stage 4 Cancer, Pike Place Decides to Increase Our Chances of Being Hit By a Car
articles.author: Vivian McCall
paras: War is back: The US and Iran exchanged missiles for the first time since late July. After we claimed to hit two rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz (claiming they were just about to fire missiles carrying naval mines toward the water), Iran struck US bases in Jordan and American military assets in the United Arab Emirates. Iran says our attacks killed and wounded several of its soldiers and civilians. In a feat of verbal hopscotch, the US denies that firing a missile was an act of aggression. It was, of course, a “limited, precise action.”

Speaking of precise: The humanitarian pacifists at Lockheed Martin claim their ballistic missile of the future, the Lockheed Martin Precision Strike Missile, is lethal, long-range and pinpoint. As we have seen since it was first deployed in combat on the first day of our war on Iran, a weapon designed to explode in midair and “propel tens of thousands of dense metal pellets at high speed in all directions” is not pinpoint. Three missiles that struck the city of Lamerd in southern Iran killed civilians 164 feet away from the impact zone.

In apparent defense of the homeland, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents arrested 76-year-old Loreto Javar, a green card holder with Stage 4 prostate cancer during an interview for US Citizenship. He has been detained at the Northwest Detention Center in Tacoma for two months. A retired hotel worker who lives in Fife with his wife and daughter, Javar has no criminal history in the US and has lived here for more than 30 years. In federal court documents, the US government alleges that in the 1970s, Javar spent three years in jail in the Philippines after an “altercation” that left a man dead, the Seattle Times reports .

Authorities claim Javar did not disclose his conviction when he moved to the US to join his father in 1995, which would have made him “inadmissible” at the time. He is “therefore ineligible to remain in the United States now,” ICE said in a statement. Javar’s family and activists want him released. Medical neglect is commonplace in ICE detainment , including untreated cancer. He’s already getting his meals late, which makes it difficult to take his cancer medication on time.

On Friday night, Dolly Parton fans held a candlelit vigil and sing-along to honor their dearly departed queen. “When I heard that Dolly passed, I was just so hungry to be with other people,” vigil organizer Francesca Hays told KUOW’s Casey Martin . “She was the epitome of love and light, and what you want people to be,” said attendee Andrea Leuser, who wore a sparkling, flowing dress and pink butterfly hair clips, “and 80 just wasn’t long enough for a woman like that.”

Five people are dead after a head-on collision 11 miles north of East Wenatchee on State Route 2 late Sunday. Near milepost 137, a westbound Nissan Maxima crossed into the eastbound lanes, slamming head-on into a 2015 Chevrolet Sonic. The male driver of the Nissan and his three male passengers were killed. Two were not wearing seat belts. The driver of the Sonic, a 77-year-old woman, was also killed. The Washington State Patrol says drugs or alcohol were involved.
In South Seattle, a shooting on the 1200 Block of SW Holden Street and Delridge Sunday evening left a 21-year-old in serious condition . The man was taken to Harborview.

One person is dead and 15 are missing after a flash flood at Grand Canyon National Park, reports the Washington Post . At least 62 people were evacuated by air after the flood hit around 2:30 p.m. Sunday afternoon. None of the evacuated were injured. The National Park Service is “seeking information” about hikers, backpackers, and people with camping reservations in affected parts of the canyon a day before the flood.

Walkers, do not rejoice! Last week, the Pike Place Historic Commission unanimously approved the next phase of the pedestrian pilot program, curtailing vehicle access to the market on Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays from October through March. If you’re not clued in, this may sound neat, but, it’s the commission bringing back car access five times a week for the first time in 18 months, despite the pedestrian pilot boosting attendance and sales , two things businesses adore. The Urbanist has more .

I know that some of you derive a near-orgasmic pleasure from leaving your Lime bikes and scooters wherever the fuck, but please consider the deafblind people tripping over them . “Safety needs to be number one,” said Mae Lynn Mullen, a Columbia City resident who is deaf and has visual impairment, told the Emerald through a sign language interpreter. “It’s come to a point where [multiple] scooters or bikes are turned over at a four-way intersection, and people are just walking over them and around them. I don’t accept that. We can do better.”
Weather : Mostly sunny with a high of 72. Near perfect. The sky is blindingly blue. The rain may come Tuesday night and it’ll almost certainly be here by Wednesday.

articles.title: Trump’s plan to sell off a part of Yosemite is what oligarchy looks like | Rebecca Solnit
articles.author: Rebecca Solnit
paras: Public lands belong to all of us. No one should plunder those lands for profit

Do people still say a car was “sold for parts”? Because the US is being sold for parts or just handed over to the oligarchy. It’s a fire sale, a bankruptcy auction, it’s a planned dismantling of everything from its military to its institutions of higher education to its scientific research to its public lands.

And while the threat to sell off part of Yosemite national park is about a quarter-mile parcel on the park’s edge, Yosemite is a crown jewel in the national park system and, arguably, the world’s first national park.

Rebecca Solnit is a Guardian US columnist. She is the author of Orwell’s Roses and co-editor with Thelma Young Lutunatabua of the climate anthology Not Too Late: Changing the Climate Story from Despair to Possibility

articles.title: Caregiver creep: how helping elderly relatives can snowball into a full-time job
articles.author: Laura House
paras: Assisting an ageing loved one can start with small tasks but may lead to full-time caregiving that requires more support
Helping an ageing parent or loved one often begins with easy-to-field requests: Pick up a prescription. Drive them to a doctor’s appointment. Grab groceries.

However, light tasks – just “helping out” here and there – may eventually snowball into the avalanche of full-time caregiving, a phenomenon becoming known as “caregiver creep”. Like “ caregiver burnout ”, it’s not a formal term, but there is growing awareness about this slow build among healthcare providers and experts.

It was among the defining moments of the 2026 World Cup: Lionel Messi standing arms akimbo, looking up towards Argentina’s fervent supporters after losing the final . Tears streamed down his face after his team’s embarrassing loss to Spain in what we now know was Messi’s final match wearing that famous Argentina kit.

It was not the first time he’d cried at the tournament. There had been tears of joy in Argentina’s opening match, when Messi rolled back the clock to his glory days with a trio of spectacular goals against Algeria. There had been more when his brace against Austria pushed Argentina through to the knockout round as group winners, and even more when his equalizer against Egypt threw la Albiceleste a much-needed lifeline. paras: Since it was stripped of planetary status, Pluto’s defenders have been fighting the decision – and they’re only getting more passionate

Twenty years ago, Pluto got demoted. After a vote by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) in August 2006, Pluto was relegated from major planet to dwarf planet status. Our solar system dropped from nine planets to eight. At the time, many scientists were unhappy with the decision. Two decades on, the debate is, if anything, even more polarised.

“The definition of a planet they created, you can’t use it at all,” says Philip Metzger, the director of the Stephen W Hawking Centre for Microgravity Research and Education at the University of Central Florida. “It makes the definition of a planet completely non-useful in science.”
