articles.title: Floods in Nepal-Tibet disrupt pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, a sacred mountain with centuries of evolving tradition
articles.author:
<name>Catherine Hartmann, Associate Professor of Religious Studies, University of Wyoming</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/catherine-hartmann-2761165"/>
paras: Hundreds of pilgrims traveling to Mount Kailash were among those affected by devastating floods that struck the Nepal–Tibet border on Aug. 26, 2026. The floods destroyed the border crossing most commonly used to reach what is arguably the most revered holy mountain in the world, which sits in the Tibet autonomous region of China.

Hindus know the peak as the dwelling place of the god Shiva , Tibetan Buddhists as the abode of the deity Demchok , and Jains as the site where Rishabhanatha , their first spiritual teacher, achieved liberation. Today it also draws nonreligious travelers, who come for the harsh beauty of the landscape and the difficulty of the journey itself. Pilgrims and travelers do not climb Kailash. Instead, they walk a path roughly 33 miles around its base, which many believe to provide blessings and purification.

The legend of Kailash goes back thousands of years, to ancient Indian traditions describing a mountain at the center of the universe. But for most of that history, the Kailash of Indian literature was not associated with the peak that pilgrims travel to now.

In 2025, I published a book about Tibetan pilgrimage to Kailash . While researching it, I learned that it took centuries for a mythical mountain to become identified with this particular peak in western Tibet.

Indian religious texts describe a range of snowy mountains to the north called the Himalaya, or “abode of snows.” Beyond them, Indian cosmologies described a cosmic mountain called Meru, believed to stand at the center of the world .

The historian Alex McKay writes that the earliest mentions of a mountain named Kailash – Kailasa in Sanskrit – appear in the Hindu epics, composed roughly between the 4th century B.C.E. and the 4th century C.E.

In the “ Ramayana ,” an epic recounting of the god-king Rama’s search for his abducted wife, the monkey king Sugriva describes the far-off north, including Mount Kailash and Mount Meru . In the “ Mahabharata ,” an epic of dynastic war, the prince Arjuna visits a hermitage located on Mount Kailash .

However, these epics do not provide a specific location for Kailash. They portray it as a forbidding mountain realm of sages and gods, not as a pilgrimage destination for humans. The Mahabharata lists sacred places pilgrims should visit – sites across northern and western India – but Kailash is not among them. In fact, the epic states repeatedly that mere mortals cannot travel to the Himalayas .

It is in the “ Puranas ,” a body of Hindu religious texts composed between roughly the 3rd and 10th centuries, that Kailash is described as the abode of Shiva. The Puranas also begin to describe Kailash as the earthly form of the divine Meru . But it is still not a place of pilgrimage and still not fixed to a particular point on the map.

Eventually, though scholars do not know exactly when, local traditions in North India began to identify particular peaks as Kailash. At least five different mountains , in the states of Jammu, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, have been claimed as the Kailash, and local pilgrimage to them continues today.

As Buddhism spread from India to Tibet beginning in the 7th century, Tibetans inherited Buddhist scriptures that spoke of Meru, Kailash and other sacred mountains. They also had their own long-standing practices of mountain veneration , making offerings to mountains that were believed to be the homes of local deities. Among them was the mountain now known as Kailash in western Tibet.

Tibetan traditions record that the geographical site of Kailash was claimed by practitioners of more than one religious tradition, and that the 11th-century saint Milarepa converted it to being a Buddhist site after defeating a non-Buddhist rival in a contest of magical power.

In the centuries that followed, Kailash became known as a particularly auspicious place to meditate and to visit on pilgrimage. Tibetans believed that while the mountain was the dwelling place of the deity Demchok, its true nature was only visible to the spiritually advanced . Any pilgrim who visited Kailash, known to Tibetans as Gang Rinpoche, would obtain blessings.
Even in Tibet, however, Kailash was only one pilgrimage site among many. Far more pilgrims visited the capital city of Lhasa .

The first clear reference to Indian Hindu pilgrims visiting the Tibetan Kailash comes in 1670, according to McKay , although earlier visits are possible. Its identity as the Kailash was not fully settled until the Indian subcontinent came under British colonial rule in the 19th century. Geographic surveyors mapping the border regions traced the sources of rivers such as the Indus to areas near Kailash. This matched ancient descriptions of Kailash as giving rise to rivers , and so the identification stuck.
By the 19th century, a small but steady flow of pilgrims traveled from India and Nepal, usually alongside the trade caravans crossing the Himalayan passes .

After China asserted control over Tibet in 1950, China and India negotiated official pilgrimage routes in a 1954 agreement . That arrangement did not last long. In 1959, a Tibetan uprising against Chinese rule was suppressed, and the Dalai Lama – the spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism – fled to India; religious life inside Tibet was severely restricted in the following years. In 1962, India and China fought a war over their disputed border, after which the border closed to Indian pilgrims for nearly two decades.

Routes reopened in 1981, and Tibetans were permitted to resume pilgrimage as well. But since then many Tibetans have found it difficult to obtain the necessary permits , and others have criticized excessive construction of hotels and roads at Kailash .

Most pilgrims today travel with private tour companies. Demand this year ran well above the Chinese government’s quota of 24,000 permits for Indian pilgrims . The Indian government also sponsors an official pilgrimage, with participants chosen by lottery, but places are limited to 1,000 people. Pilgrimage by Indian travelers had reopened only in 2025, after being suspended since 2020 because of COVID-19 and a deadly clash between Indian and Chinese troops in the Galwan Valley over the still-disputed India-China border.

Today, Kailash receives more pilgrims than at any point in its history. Most travelers from India now fly to Kathmandu and continue by bus through Gyirong, a road crossing between Nepal and Tibet that was expanded in 2014 and opened to international travelers in 2017 . It became the most popular route after the 2015 earthquake damaged the main alternative. It was this crossing that the August 26 floods destroyed.

articles.title: Federal stimulus money bought new technology for Philly students, but many schools lost track of where items went
articles.author:
<name>Suzanne McLeod, Assistant Professor of Educational Leadership, Binghamton University, State University of New York</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/suzanne-mcleod-836387"/>
paras: Back-to-school season is underway, and school personnel have been busy cleaning, doing repairs and setting up classrooms for the 2026-27 academic year. This work includes making sure appropriate supplies and equipment are there for the students.

For the past two years, Philadelphia’s city controller’s office has cited the School District of Philadelphia for its poor accountability of capital assets . Capital assets are items with a useful life of over one year and that cost at least US$5,000. They include items such as pianos, laptops and smartboards, to name just a few.
Across its schools, the Philadelphia school district holds over $2.8 billion in capital assets, according to the most recent Annual Financial Comprehensive Report .

The controller’s office found that over 60% of the assets it tested in school locations had not been properly recorded in the official ledgers and were unable to be located. Its February 2026 report listed the numerous items by school building. These items included printers, computers and even a lunchroom table.

These findings don’t necessarily mean that a large percentage of assets were definitely lost or stolen; it is often the case that items are moved or disposed of and not properly recorded. But the findings indicate a systemic problem with recording, tracking and disposing of assets.

We are former school leaders in New York state public school districts. One of us was a superintendent of schools from 2008-2019 and the other was a regional school district controller from 2013-2024 in central New York. In these roles, we worked together, with the Board of Education and our administrative team, to build and test policies and procedures for the purchasing, inventorying and auditing of school equipment. We wanted to make sure that all school district assets were accounted for and available for student learning.

Today, we teach aspiring school leaders how to lead all aspects of education programs from pre-K through high school. This includes the business functions of running public schools, such as fulfilling legal, regulatory and policy requirements.
Purchasing goods and services is a highly regulated area in U.S. public school districts.

Federal regulations require districts that receive federal funds to maintain control over assets, track purchases, conduct regular inventory of assets and maintain documentation related to purchases and disposals.

During recent reviews of Education Stabilization Fund spending, many districts across the country were found to lack appropriate inventorying of purchases, which is in direct violation of federal procurement requirements. One of us participated in 15 of those reviews; all 15 lacked appropriate inventorying.

Pennsylvania’s Department of Labor and Industry laws and regulations , as well as Philadelphia’s Board of Education , also require accurate inventory records and periodic updates of asset locations, additions, transfers and disposals.

In short, the district has to record the purchase of any capital asset that cost $5,000 or more if it has a useful life of more than one year. These assets and other noncapital items – which are items with a useful life of over one year but cost under $5,000 – must be inventoried by the department responsible for custody of the asset. So, for example, the information technology department is responsible for recording and tracking Chromebooks and iPads, while the special education department would record and track audio equipment purchased for students with special needs.

Local governments, such as Philadelphia schools, are also governed by the Governmental Accounting Standards Board, which issues rules on financial transactions and reporting. Accounting Statement 34 from the standards-setting nonprofit lays the foundation for capitalizing, reporting and depreciating capital assets.

The COVID-19 pandemic that began in March 2020 had a massive impact on students, schools and school districts. A 2023 analysis of almost 600 studies focused on the impact of school closures reported that students lost about 3 ½ months of instruction.
As schools reopened for in-person learning, school districts across the U.S. received federal stimulus funds to, among other priorities, close this learning gap.
Philadelphia public schools received a total of $1.8 billion in federal stimulus funds between 2020 and 2024 to upgrade facilities and support academic recovery.

The money was spent on everything from new laptops and tablets to upgraded heating, ventilating, and air conditioning systems and furniture, as well as items like weighted blankets and noise-canceling headphones to address the social and emotional needs of children. The spike in purchases presented challenges when it came to inventorying assets, as a lot of dollars had to be spent quickly within specified grant periods.

Based on the findings of the controller’s report, the Philadelphia school district either lacked systems that were strong enough to track, safeguard and reconcile what it bought, or the district did not use the system properly. The findings state that the district’s decentralized approach to recording assets, with capital assets tracked centrally and noncapital assets tracked by departments or schools, contributed to the issue.

The New York state public schools had their own reckoning following a 2004 story, broken by a high school student newspaper, of over $11 million being embezzled by district officials from the Roslyn Union Free School District.

The fallout of this fraud included several new state-level fiscal accountability reforms for all New York school districts, including stricter internal controls, mandatory board oversight and independent auditor requirements. This is the structure we worked under as school district leaders. While stringent, we were able to develop and implement systems and procedures that allowed our students access to the equipment they needed to learn.
Consistent systems, clear policies and processes, and focused accountability can go a long way.

Based on this experience, we believe there are steps that every pre-K to 12 public school district in Pennsylvania and across the country can do to improve their systems for tracking school equipment:
Districts can set up structures that allow the purchasing department and the receiving departments to work together on appropriately tagging all new equipment.

Electronic inventory systems, like barcodes, can be expanded to allow for timely updates to capital assets and noncapital inventories to keep better track of equipment, such as if an item is transferred to a different location or becomes damaged and is sent out for repair.

District leaders can require that each department, from school buildings to centralized technology and special education departments, certify their inventory each year and identify any missing assets. Stringent follow-up on areas of noncompliance can be addressed by the business office.
Robust training for all school personnel on how to purchase and track assets and inventory items can help ensure compliance. This might include standardized materials and recorded how-to videos.
The Philadelphia school board’s vision is to prepare students to imagine and realize any future they desire. Strong asset management systems can help ensure that the vision becomes reality.

articles.title: Trust is a behavior, not a credential – and that explains the Rodgers-Fauci divide
articles.author:
<name>John C. Besley, Professor of Public Relations, Michigan State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/john-c-besley-153042"/>
paras: Following an appearance on The Pat McAfee Show on Aug. 3, 2026, Aaron Rodgers, quarterback for the Pittsburgh Steelers, received attention for calling Dr. Anthony Fauci an “absolute coward” and “criminal.” Rodgers’ comments were in response to Fauci invoking his Fifth Amendment rights at a congressional hearing on pandemic-era policies and the origins of COVID-19.

Fauci exercised his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination more than 100 times, rather than answer questions about his role in the government’s pandemic response. The invocation came amid years of congressional investigations and hearings scrutinizing his handling of the pandemic.

Fauci’s testimony likely didn’t do much to build public trust – invoking the Fifth Amendment dozens of times may have read as evasive even when it’s legally sound, and the format didn’t help either. Congressional hearings and press briefings aren’t, by design, places where people show much of themselves. Rodgers, on the other hand, has spent years doing the opposite – speaking candidly and often, in settings built for exactly that kind of rapport-building.

This isn’t unique to Rodgers. Many public figures – athletes, influencers, podcast hosts – have more regular opportunities to build rapport with audiences than experts do, at a time when Americans express decreased trust in experts overall.

There’s a reason for that decreased trust. Trust research can both help make sense of why someone might pay attention to a football player’s opinion of the former head of The National Institutes of Health. But that research also highlights the limits of opinion surveys that simply ask people how much they trust various groups in society .

These “how much do you trust” questions probe Americans’ overall views of specific groups , like scientists. The issue is that these questions sidestep deeper discussions about what makes people willing to put their trust in others.
Many researchers, including me , study the intersection of trust and how scientists engage the public. One thing essential to understanding trust is to separate behaviors from beliefs.

Trust researchers often treat trust as a type of behavior rather than an overall evaluation about a group. When it comes to healthcare, this might mean looking at how willing people are to follow their doctor’s medical advice. It matters less whether people say they trust doctors on a survey and more how they behave in their daily lives.
Trust behaviors involve making yourself vulnerable to someone else , and such behaviors are everywhere in our lives, once you know to look for them.

People demonstrate trust in automakers, mechanics, government employees who regulate and police roadways, and even other drivers by choosing to drive. People also demonstrate trust in economists, ecologists and epidemiologists, when they consider their advice while making personal or civic decisions.
Defining trust as a type of behavior helps clarify the key question: What beliefs make people more likely to trust?

Understanding what researchers often call trustworthiness beliefs – sometimes called perceptions – can help experts understand where they are falling short, whether in their behaviors or in how they communicate.
Scholars have long known that people don’t just trust scientists because they believe they hold expertise . What people believe about others’ character also matters.
While some research focuses on beliefs about expertise and character, other trust frameworks break character into smaller parts.
Benevolence beliefs can be understood as feeling that someone has goodwill toward you and cares about your well-being. Integrity beliefs focus on expectations about honesty and morality.

For example, a scientist might show a real desire to help, but fail to show how they protect their work’s integrity – like by being transparent about a study’s limitations or disclosing potential conflicts of interest. Likewise, an expert might demonstrate integrity without communicating care for the people that their decisions might affect.
Some researchers consider other character attributes too. Two common ones include beliefs about whether someone will listen and share information and whether someone shares your values .
These distinctions matter for experts who want to earn trust because the actions needed to demonstrate one aspect of trustworthiness may not demonstrate other aspects.

For example, experts might put a lot of effort into listening to community needs to demonstrate integrity and openness, but miss opportunities to communicate the underlying benevolent motivations driving their work. A public health department might hold listening sessions before rolling out a new program, but if it doesn’t also explain why it’s investing in that program – what it’s trying to protect people from, and who benefits – residents may come away seeing a checkbox exercise rather than genuine care.
Another challenge: Trustworthiness beliefs depend heavily on context . This is easy to see with expertise beliefs. The expertise you look for in a mechanic differs from what you look for in a doctor.

Trustworthiness beliefs also aren’t the only thing that shapes whether someone follows expert advice. Behavior change research points to other factors – like whether people believe an action actually benefits them, whether it’s socially accepted among their friends and family, and whether they feel capable of doing it.
In other words, someone might trust Fauci and still not get vaccinated, if they don’t believe the shot benefits them or don’t think they can manage the side effects.
Experts cannot assume that others see them as trustworthy or that people will pay attention to them while ignoring sources who have demonstrated other aspects of trustworthiness.
Experts also cannot assume people will pay close attention to every choice they’re asked to make or the trustworthiness of every information source.
People may also often rely on the most available information or follow potentially misleading cues like how compelling someone sounds, their appearance or existing beliefs.

Camera-ready influencers who interact regularly with audiences and health gurus who spend substantial time with their clients have many opportunities to shape beliefs about their ability, benevolence and integrity that busy experts cannot easily match.

These examples point to the reality that bona fide experts need to take advantage of every opportunity to demonstrate trustworthiness in engaging ways. This way, trustworthiness beliefs already exist when people make choices and when encountering potential causes for concern like Fauci’s testimony.

I often advise scientists to be more proactive in demonstrating their motivations and how they protect their work’s integrity while avoiding choices that may communicate a lack of concern or shared values .

articles.title: Indictments against a top extremism researcher and the SPLC force a reckoning on research ethics – an extremism scholar reflects on the field’s challenges
articles.author:
<name>Arie Perliger, Director of Security Studies and Professor of Criminology and Justice Studies, UMass Lowell</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/arie-perliger-379619"/>
paras: The August 2026 federal indictment of Heidi Beirich , a longtime researcher who studies political violence and the American far right, has provoked strong reactions within the professional community of extremism scholars.

I am one of those researchers . Beirich is a longtime colleague. In her work, she testified before Congress , shaped the understanding of journalists and politicians regarding organized hate groups in the United States, and collaborated with many scholars in the field.

Here’s the background: On Aug. 12 federal prosecutors unsealed a superseding indictment against Beirich , who is the former director of the Intelligence Project , the monitoring and research arm of the Southern Poverty Law Center, for wire fraud, bank fraud and money laundering. The indictment follows the April indictment of the SPLC itself , an Alabama-based civil rights nonprofit that has spent five decades litigating against white supremacist organizations and cataloging hate groups through its widely cited “ hate map .”

The April indictment accused the organization of secretly funneling millions of dollars in donor funds to informants embedded in violent extremist movements, using bank accounts opened for fictitious companies.

The SPLC cases raise a crucial question for extremism researchers: In a field whose research methods can at times diverge from standard and approved methods in other academic areas, what are the legitimate ethical limits, especially with respect to cultivation of insider sources and source compensation?
I believe that a field that documents how political movements rationalize the misconduct of their own members should be the last to reproduce this pattern.
For decades, the SPLC’s Intelligence Project tracked far-right extremist organizations . Some of that knowledge came from public sources, but some of it came from people inside those movements.
To understand how clandestine groups actually operate, who leads them, where they meet and what they are planning, the organization cultivated insiders and, according to prosecutors, paid them.

The SPLC maintains in its court filings that information gathered this way was shared with federal law enforcement , including in the period surrounding the 2017 “Unite the Right” rally in Charlottesville, Va. The Justice Department disputes that characterization.
What is not in dispute is that this practice existed, and its legality is the center of the case against both the SPLC and Beirich.

The indictment alleges that the SPLC misrepresented to donors how their contributions would be used, that it opened bank accounts in the names of fictitious entities to disguise the source and destination of the payments, and that between 2007 and 2023 more than US$4 million reached individuals connected to the Ku Klux Klan, Aryan Nations, the National Alliance, the United Klans of America and participants in the Unite the Right rally.

In Beirich’s case specifically, prosecutors allege that roughly $140,000 moved between 2015 and 2021 from an SPLC account into accounts she jointly held with an informant, and that the money covered personal living expenses.
Beirich, through her attorneys, has firmly rejected the accusations as politically motivated.
Indeed, there is a politicized context surrounding the prosecution. This was reflected both in the administration’s statements and actions against the SPLC.

On the day of the April indictment, Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said the SPLC had been “manufacturing racism to justify its existence” and was “ manufacturing the extremism it purports to oppose .”

Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon described the prosecution as “personal,” citing her own prior representation of people the SPLC had labeled extremists , which Dhillon believed was unjustified.

The FBI decided in October 2025 to end its cooperation with the SPLC , which had involved sharing data and analysis on hate crimes and hate groups and drawing on the organization’s tracking of extremist movements.

In early August 2026, a federal judge denied the SPLC’s motion to dismiss the organization’s indictment as a vindictive prosecution , finding that it had not produced objective evidence tying the political criticism to the charging decision itself. She also refused to let the organization obtain the government’s internal records of how the decision to prosecute was reached, describing its submissions as “ speculation upon conjecture .” Days later, Beirich was charged in the second superseding indictment.
These two cases force researchers to grapple with how knowledge about violent movements is actually produced.
Researchers, journalists and watchdog organizations rely on four broad avenues of access:

• Consent-based engagement , which consists primarily of interviews with current and former members of extremist movements, conducted under institutional oversight and with informed consent, meaning that participants are told what the research is for, what will be done with what they say, and that they may withdraw at any point.
• Observational fieldwork , which includes attending rallies, meetings and public events to document organizational dynamics.
• Large-scale collection of online content from platforms and encrypted channels where extremist communities organize and communicate.

• Cultivation of insider sources – by far the most delicate information collection. Sources include defectors, informants and individuals who remain embedded within movements while passing information to outsiders. Academic researchers rarely use this last avenue. Watchdog organizations and investigative journalists rely on it.
Academic research on human subjects is governed by a framework built largely in response to past medical and psychological research abuses .

Its core commitments are voluntary and informed participation, minimization of harm to participants, confidentiality and prior approval by an institutional review board that weighs risk against scientific value. That architecture assumes a research setting in which the participant is the vulnerable party, the risks are foreseeable and the researcher is safe.
Extremism research fits none of those assumptions cleanly.
Covert observation conflicts with informed consent . Revealing oneself to a violent movement can put the researcher in danger and skew the data.
Information collected for academic purposes can acquire operational value for law enforcement agencies, blurring the line between research and intelligence work .

And the compensation of sources exists in the deepest gray area of all. Mainstream journalism largely prohibits paying sources . Law enforcement institutionalizes it through regulated informant programs .

However, researchers and watchdog organizations operate in the unregulated space between these poles. Paying an insider may be the only way to maintain access, protect the source or extract someone from a movement, but that same payment also carries the risk of subsidizing the movement itself.
The field has never resolved this tension and largely avoided it.

The Framework for Research Ethics in Terrorism Studies gives review boards a structured set of questions covering participant vulnerability, consent, anonymity, data security and the safety of the researcher. But it addresses how researchers should be reviewed rather than how insider relationships should be financed. On the question of paying a source, the framework, like the field, remains largely silent.

If courts accept the government’s legal approach in the SPLC cases, effectively treating discreet payment channels to insider sources as inherently fraudulent, the implications reach far beyond a single organization.

Watchdog groups and newsrooms that route payments through intermediaries to keep a source’s identity insulated in dangerous reporting environments, and researchers who compensate participants for their time under routine institutional review board approval, would all find their standard methods newly exposed.

That will undermine efforts to gain a clear picture of violent extremism in the U.S., including how many attacks occur and by whom, how movements recruit, how online spaces convert grievance into planning and which warning signs precede violence.

That work feeds federal and state threat assessments, informs social media platforms on how to identify extremist users and content, shapes prevention programs and supplies the evidentiary basis for prosecutions and congressional oversight. A legal theory that treats discreet payment channels to insider sources as inherently fraudulent would narrow the range of what can be known about movements that conceal themselves by design.

Despite such concerns, the positive outlook is that a professional field that has spent decades documenting how political movements rationalize the misconduct of their members is in an unusually good position to notice when it starts doing the same thing.
Researchers can use this moment to finally build the ethical infrastructure around the cultivation of insider sources and source compensation that the field has postponed for too long.

articles.title: What would you see if you had one eye on the back of your head and the other in the front?
articles.author:
<name>Abigail Witmer, Assistant Clinical Professor of Optometry, The Ohio State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/abigail-witmer-2706578"/>
paras: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com .
What would my vision look like if I had one eye in front and another in back? – Mohibul, age 18, India

Have you ever tried to quickly grab that last cookie while your mother’s back was turned? Even without turning around, I bet she noticed. As the saying goes, moms can sometimes seem like they have eyes on the back of their heads.
What would their vision be like if they really did have one eye in front and one eye in back?

As an optometrist , I work daily to make sure my patients’ eyes are seeing well and partnering with one another to provide a single, clear image to the brain. As a clinical professor , I help my students understand how binocular vision – the use of two eyes – works. Sometimes, this may include using animal examples to illustrate how important it is for humans to have two eyes that face in the same direction.

As you can see by looking at yourself in the mirror, our two eyes sit side by side on the front of our heads. Since our eyes are a couple of inches apart, each eye has a slightly different perspective on the world around you.

There’s a good bit of overlap between what each eye sees, though. Close one eye at a time – you should still be able to see the words in the middle of the page with each eye individually. The words on the left side, though, might only be clear when your left eye is open, and with the same true for the right side and the right eye.

Someone with normal side vision can see about 180 degrees around them while looking straight ahead. In other words, your view of the world should be everything directly in front of you stretching back to roughly your ears — about half of a circle. This whole area that you can see at once is called your field of vision . About 70% of that field is an overlap between the images captured by each eye.
Next, your brain takes these images from each eye and combines the overlapping portion into one 3D image . The ability to see in three dimensions is called stereopsis , or depth perception.

This is how you can tell which objects in front of you are closer or farther away. Depth perception allows you to better navigate around objects and is important for hand-eye coordination. Without 3D vision, it would be hard to perform all the complicated tasks that people do in their daily lives – writing, reading, cooking, playing sports, driving and so much more.
Animals have evolved to have different eye placements based on the jobs they need their eyes to do.

For example, predators – animals that need to hunt other animals for food to survive – will have eyes on the front of their heads, just like us. This setup allows for depth perception . They will be able to more accurately scan specific areas and pick out animals that may be hiding.

Predators also tend to have more crystal clear vision and better contrast sensitivity , meaning they’re able to tell the difference between an object and its background. All of these adaptations help them hunt.

In contrast, prey animals’ job is to detect and get away from predators that are trying to eat them. They have eyes closer to the sides of their heads, which increases their side vision . This larger field of view allows them to scan a wider area to watch for incoming danger. Of note: Their vision isn’t as sharp as predators’.

A good example of a predator-prey relationship is a fox and a rabbit. The fox has forward-facing eyes to help it find and hunt the rabbit. The rabbit has eyes on the side of its head to help it scan and escape from the fox.

An owl is an example of an animal that gets the best of both worlds. Owls are predators whose eyes are positioned on the front of their heads, giving them excellent depth perception. Because of how their eyes are shaped , though, they can’t move them in their eye sockets. Instead, they have adapted to have very mobile necks so they can turn their head to be facing completely backward . This gives them a much wider field of vision than most animals with forward-facing eyes, while preserving their depth perception.
So what would it be like for us to have one eye in front and one in back?
This setup would be most similar to a prey animal. You’d have a wide field of view and be able to see almost all of your surroundings – forward and behind at the same time.
But the cost would be loss of depth perception. With eyes on opposite sides of your head, the images they capture would not overlap, causing your vision to be less three-dimensional.

Also, if the switch from side by side to one-front/one-back happened instantaneously, your brain would get confused about how to interpret the images delivered from each eye, since the setup would be quite different from what you were used to.
In my patients, especially kids, my goal is to make sure their vision is clear and their eyes are working together to achieve depth perception.

If your eyes ever have trouble pointing in the same direction , or you notice double vision or eyestrain when reading, headaches, or other visual symptoms, visit an eye care specialist to check your eyes. They can make sure you are using your eyes the way evolution intended – two eyes in the front of the head working together for clear, binocular vision. It’s important to keep your forward-facing eyes healthy – especially if you’re a mom who needs to watch out for cookie bandits.

Hello, curious kids! Do you have a question you’d like an expert to answer? Ask an adult to send your question to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com . Please tell us your name, age and the city where you live.
And since curiosity has no age limit – adults, let us know what you’re wondering, too. We won’t be able to answer every question, but we will do our best.

articles.title: Worms navigate narrow paths faster than wide ones – these findings could inform robot design
articles.author:
<name>K. R. Prathyusha, Research Associate, BioFrontiers Institute, University of Colorado Boulder</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/k-r-prathyusha-2745344"/>
paras: You might naturally expect a wide, open path to be faster and easier to navigate than a narrow one, just as birds fly freely through the open sky, cars move quickly on empty roads, and a wide hallway seems easier when trying to exit a building.

However, many organisms do not have the option to move through open spaces. Whether burrowing through soil or swimming through water, they’re forced to maneuver through narrow gaps in tiny pores, rocks, roots, plants or other obstacles.
My team’s recent research on California blackworms suggests that, sometimes, such narrower paths are faster . And these findings could have implications for building specialized robots.

I’m a physicist who studies living systems. I work in Saad Bhamla’s lab , where we ask simple questions about nature and uncover the rich physics behind them. Being part of the lab often reminds me of my childhood in Kerala, India, where I spent countless hours outdoors watching and playing with the tiny organisms around me. My research brings me the same sense of wonder, only now as a physicist.

One of the most extensively studied organisms in our lab is the California blackworm, Lumbriculus variegatus . In groups, these aquatic worms, roughly a few-centimeters long, weave themselves into tangled structures that resemble bundles of thread or noodles in a bowl, but are alive.

For one project, our group investigated how collections of worms behave under confinement, through experiments led by Ph.D. student Paulami Sarkar . During our discussions, I began wondering whether we could build a simple computational model that captured the essential physics that tangled these worms together.
Justin Xu, an undergraduate student whom I was mentoring in computational research, joined the project, and together we decided to explore this question through computer simulations.

As a first step, we started with the simplest possible system by simulating a single worm moving through two channels. Each channel had a length twice that of the worm, but the two had different widths: one about as wide as the worm’s diameter, and another much wider than its diameter.

Our computational model is much simpler than a real worm. It has no muscles, no nervous system and none of the complexity of a living organism. It retains only two essential ingredients: a long, flexible chain and the ability to propel itself forward .

Imagine this chain as a string of tiny beads connected together. Now imagine that each bead carries a tiny battery that continuously gives it a gentle push along the chain. Together, these tiny pushes make the entire chain bend, wriggle and move much like a real worm.
Because both a real worm and our computational model were flexible, self-propelled filaments, or “ active filaments ,” we could use the same physical principles to study how they move.
One day, I noticed something unexpected. The simulated worm was consistently moving through the narrower channel faster than the wider one. The more I thought about it, the more puzzling it became.

In physics, the process of moving through a confined channel or pore is known as translocation. Researchers have extensively studied translocation in the context of long, flexible molecules called polymers, one of the best-known examples being DNA .

DNA is a long, threadlike molecule that often passes through tiny pores in biological membranes, both inside living cells and in modern DNA-sequencing technologies. Because DNA has less room to bend and change shape inside these narrow pores, tighter confinement generally slows its motion.

California blackworms, however, are very different from DNA. They continuously propel themselves forward by contracting and bending their long, flexible bodies. In physics, such systems are called active matter . Active matter can range from swimming bacteria and migrating cells to flocks of birds , schools of fish and self-propelled robots .

The unexpected result from computer simulations opened up a series of questions. Was it merely an artifact of our computational model, or would a California blackworm also move faster through narrower passages? And if DNA slows down in narrower pores, what makes active filaments behave so differently in confinement?

There was only one way to find out: test the idea with real California blackworms. I shared the unexpected simulation result with Sarkar and Bhamla, and they were equally excited and intrigued. Sarkar designed a series of experiments with blackworms in 12-centimeter-long (about 5 inches) channels, about twice the worm’s length. She varied the channel widths from 1 to 8 millimeters, about 2 to 16 times the diameter of a worm (which is about half a millimeter).

To our surprise, the experiments on real worms told the same story. Just like their simulated counterparts, the worms consistently moved through the narrower channels faster than the wider ones . For the channel length we tested, they took nearly three times as long to escape from the wider channels as from the narrower ones.
What began as an unexpected observation in a simple computational model had now been confirmed in a living organism.

Inside a narrow channel, the active filaments had little opportunity to turn sideways. The surrounding walls naturally kept their bodies aligned with the direction of travel, so they spent most of their time moving toward the exit, rather than changing direction.

In the wider channel, they had more room to move, so they frequently paused, bent, reoriented themselves and explored sideways before continuing their journey. These stop-and-go movements became increasingly common as the channel widened.

Greater freedom of movement, it turned out, came with a hidden cost. Every pause, bend and change in direction delayed progress . Rather than helping them reach the exit more quickly, the extra space encouraged exploratory motion.

The implications of our findings extend beyond blackworms. Engineers face similar challenges when designing flexible machines. Scientists are developing soft robots : machines made from soft, flexible materials that can bend and move like worms . These robots must navigate tight spaces while remaining flexible enough to avoid damage. The obvious engineering solution is often to remove obstacles and create more room.

Our results suggest an unexpected perspective: Confinement does not always hinder movement. For soft robots, narrower paths could sometimes be an advantage , helping future robots navigate tight spaces, whether delivering drugs or performing minimally invasive procedures inside the human body, or inspecting hard-to-reach sections of industrial pipelines.

In research, we usually choose the questions we want to answer and spend months, sometimes years, searching for answers. But every now and then, the opposite happens. An unexpected observation makes us curious and inspires us to stop and ask why.
One of the joys of science is discovering that nature often challenges our intuition.

articles.title: Sound Transit Board Greenlights Targeted Fare Gate Retrofits
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: On Thursday, the Sound Transit Board of Directors approved the creation of a fare gate retrofit program set to use $6 million that has been queued up to design a gate pilot at 14 high-ridership Link stations . Those design and planning funds are expected to ultimately turn into an $87 million program that will get gates installed by 2029 or 2030.
Once implemented, the pilot program is expected to recoup costs through higher fare compliance rates within two to three years, according to agency projections.

At last estimate, Sound Transit puts its current light rail fare compliance rate at 63%, based on automatic counters on trains compared to fares paid. The caveat: that figure includes youth under 19, who are not required to pay fares under the state's free youth fare program. Adjusting for free-ride youth would put the compliance rate closer to 70%.

Additionally, Sound Transit's fare ambassador program, which is based on staff members actually checking fares on trains, has measured the fare compliance rate at 85% in 2025, with a further 7.5% of fare-less riders checked being exempt youth. This discrepancy has led some transit advocates to argue the agency is overestimating fare evasion and the potential uptick in fare revenue that gates could prompt.

Sound Transit's financial modeling is based on achieving 95% fare compliance at stations where gates are installed, which staff noted is less that the 98% peer agencies have reported at gated stations. The need to include accessible entry points for people in wheelchairs or with strollers or bikes means the opportunity for fare gate jumping will exist to some extent, although other U.S. transit agencies have estimated that problem as a relatively minor one.

Sound Transit's initial proposal would put bi-directional fare gates at the high-ridership stations in the core of Seattle, Bellevue downtown, and at the ends of lines. Since the gates would be bidirectional and require riders to tap on to enter and tap off to exit stations, staff expect compliance rates to increase systemwide, not just at the gated stations. This is because so many trips end at the stations set to receive gates. With bi-directional gates at key stations, retrofitting all of the system's other stations down the line will likely prove much less lucrative.

"It's important to highlight that while we are showing only boardings at gated and non-gated stations, we're going to need to measure system-wide compliance given the bidirectional nature of the gates, where compliance will be driven both by boardings and alightings," said Brian de Place, Sound Transit's Security and Fare Engagement Executive Director. "And since the vast majority of our riders come in and out of the gated stations, we expect to see compliance levels change at the non-gated stations as well as the gated ones."

About 85% of Sound Transit light rail ridership starts or ends at one of the 14 gates to be targeted for gates, officials said. That traffic has grown rapidly with the extension of the 2 Line across the lake, reaching 160,000 daily riders even before the World Cup came to town.

De Place noted that the agency also opted against trying to quantify the fare compliance benefits at non-gated stations nor the side benefits they hope to achieve – such as lower maintenance costs due to less vandalism – in their financial calculations, although peer agencies, like BART, have reported such benefits after implementing fare gates. If such benefits do come to pass, the financial boost from fare gates could be even larger, he said.

Without factoring in those potential benefits, the agency estimates gates would still boost fare revenue by at least $30 million annually, an increase of more than 30% compared to today's fare revenue across the entire Sound Transit system.

While a nice little boost, that level of revenue is not likely to be large enough to be a major factor in solving the agency's multi-billion-dollar budget gap through 2046. Once estimated at $34.5 billion, the board reduced its long-term budget gap to about $10 billion in May by delaying or tabling a number of expansion projects – and planning to sunset the Sounder N Line commuter rail service. Every little bit helps, though, fare gate supporters have posited.

The fare gate pilot program received a recommendation from the Rider Experience and Operations Committee earlier this month , generating a more in-depth policy discussion at that juncture. King County Councilmember Claudia Balducci noted the agency would need to set its metrics of success for the program, which she painted as a bit squishy so far.

Some boardmembers also raised equity concerns, about potentially making it harder for low-income residents to access the light rail system. King County Executive Girmay Zahilay highlighted those concerns on Thursday, with de Place noting staff was hoping to ramp up participation in the Orca LIFT reduced fare program.

"Brian, just to clarify, you're saying that between now and when fare gates are installed in the next couple of years, we have a specific plan to set up structures or staffing where people can enroll on site for free and reduced fare cards," Zahilay said. "Is that right?"
De Place said yes, with board authorization.

As it stands, staff said about 91,000 people are enrolled in a reduced fare program. Given the Seattle metropolitan area has a population around 4 million, that suggests a fraction of the people eligible are actually enrolled in ORCA Lift or other reduced fare card programs.
In his report to the board on Thursday, Sound Transit CEO Dow Constantine pledged efforts to increase rider awareness as the roll out of the fare gate program approaches.

"Staff have heard loud and clear the emphasis on a thorough and equitable engagement strategy that ensures appropriate fare media and rider awareness materials are available to all passengers once the program is implemented," Constantine said. "Should the board adopt the pilot today, we look forward to keeping you apprised of our progress in tandem with standard design and construction updates you should expect."

After King County Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda raised a question about access for people with disabilities or with bikes in tow, Sound Transit staff assured the board the agency's Request for Proposal would factor in those needs, and that solutions existed.

"As we move into preparing the RFP and actually coming up with the design of these gates, we'll be working really closely with both the ADA community and the bike community in order to understand the specific needs of those communities vis-a-vis gates," said Meg Cederoth, who is deputy chief planning officer at Sound Transit. "And there are multiple systems in the U.S. where the ADA question has been resolved quite comfortably. We'll be making sure we're engaging with our local communities to understand any unique needs here, and then the bike community as well will be working with them to understand that the gates are wide enough."

Another aspect still to be determined is if the fare gates will be rolled out simultaneously at all 14 proposed stations, or on a rolling basis to test the program more incrementally. The board will still need to greenlight the construction funding before the pilot can fully advance.

articles.title: Op-Ed: From the Bargaining Table to Olympia, Educators Need Our Support Now
articles.author: Kelabe Tewolde
paras: It’s the last few weeks of the summer. Everyone is trying to fit in one last trip out of town, hosting cookouts, spending evenings at the lake, or like many parents diving into back to school shopping. Usually educators are gearing up and preparing to welcome back students to the classroom, but this year there is a bit of a road block.

Between now and September 2nd, the first day of school, members of Seattle Education Association (SEA) are bargaining from 9am to 9pm with Seattle Public Schools (SPS) for a fair contract. That was until last night (August 29th), when SPS walked away from the bargaining table as talks broke down regarding cuts to special education.

On August 26th, SEA authorized a strike. This doesn’t necessarily mean they will strike, but SEA’s bargaining team has the greenlight. With the district walking away from the bargaining table it is increasingly likely SEA will have their third strike in 11 years. We are just a few days away from the start of the school year, and you may be asking, “What’s the hold up?”

SEA has agreed to 12 of 57 issues and struggle to find common ground on what holds the most weight in these negotiations, centering the experience of their students and members. They have found that pressurization and wages are where the district and SEA are unable to come to an agreement. You may be wondering, what this actually means. Teachers are focused on pressurization, a.k.a. increased workload. Pressurization comes in the forms of increases in caseload, class size, and other demands that take their time and focus away from students and lead to educator burnout.

When we constantly put more and more on our educators' plates, we limit the time and energy they have to actually teach our children. And when we talk about wages, we mean making sure all SPS employees can afford to live in the city where they work. In a city as expensive as Seattle, many of the lower-paid workers are finding it difficult to afford to live here in the communities they serve. Educators are not looking for a massive raise in this contract. It is simply a cost-of-living adjustment that will ease the burden of affordability.
If I were to simplify that for the everyday person not at the bargaining table: Teachers want to improve working conditions because their working conditions are their students' learning conditions.
SEA is digging into the district’s annual $1.3 billion budget and finding that part of the problem is state funding. And part of the problem is misplaced priorities.
What is SEA fighting for beyond pressurization and wages?

Special education students have a civil right to a high-quality education : That means we need to meet their individual education plan (IEP). With more students with IEPs in general education, SPS needs to ensure that the co-teaching models are effective. Teachers need an opportunity and space in their schedule to collaborate and help ALL of their students succeed. In these co-teaching models, SPS needs to have a plan to fill in for vacancies and leaves so students with IEPs have teachers with a Special Education endorsement. This is not only an issue around providing a high quality education for all our students, but it is a civil rights issue.

Reasonable class sizes: This is critical to how students succeed. Currently, SEA’s contract includes overage pay as an incentive for the district to keep class sizes a reasonable size, but we are hearing from educators that they don’t want that overage pay. On a personal note, my friend that teaches in a different district similarly had overage pay for having a large class. Mid-year, she had to advocate to split the class up because the learning environment in a class of 35 students was not conducive to student success.

Smaller class sizes give educators the ability to connect with students and help them succeed. SEA states: “We need to create a true cap, beyond which the district must add staff or reduce the class size to ensure students have the opportunity to learn.”
Beyond class sizes, SEA has a variety of other proposals that include safety, AI usage in the classroom, and substitute reimbursement.
Long term, we need solutions from the state
These issues could be solved at the state level if we had a legislature that would prioritize the learning conditions of our children.

In 2014, we had the opportunity to implement smaller class sizes through I-1351 , providing students with one-on-one attention from caring and qualified teachers and support staff. While voters backed smaller class sizes, the state legislature unfortunately left the initiative unfunded, and in 2015 the state legislature delayed its implementation. Eventually in 2017, the legislature repealed the cap on class sizes, due to a lack of funding, leading us to the mess we are in now: Large class sizes, teachers without the resources to effectively serve their students, and students failed by a system that they simply inherited.

Teachers are burnt out and it reflects in how many educators are leaving our schools. One special education teacher told me that: “Last year was the worst teacher year of my life due to an unsustainable and unsupported SpEd caseload. And every SpEd teacher in my building except one left at the end of last year. It’s leading to massive burnout and attrition.”
Without proper class sizes and support, we are failing our teachers, and in turn failing our children.
Many critics to this solution will bring up, “if smaller class sizes were unfunded in 2014, how would you fund them now, especially with an upcoming austerity budget?”

Well, simply put, we would need to reform our tax code like WEA recommended about a decade ago. I’m writing this off the heels of Washington State coming in as No. 1 — for corporate tax breaks and corporations like Microsoft paying a tax rate of 2.4%, while people that earn less than $33,500 a year have a tax rate of 13.8% . We need a legislature that is bold enough to stand up for our values and provide a quality education for all, while creating a sensible tax code that makes everyone pay their fair share .

And this November, we have a choice in legislative races all over the state. We need to elect legislators that are willing to balance the tax code. We deserve legislators who will stand with workers over corporate profits. And legislators that support our educators all year long, not just during an election year.

In the upcoming days, I ask you to support our teachers. This could be showing up for the bargaining team at rallies, spreading the word via social media, calling on the district to meet SEA’s proposals , and, if there is a strike, picketing with teachers throughout the city demanding SPS meet their proposals.

articles.title: Bill Gates in his own words: How he’s using AI, and why he’s worried about the future
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: This week on the GeekWire Podcast: Bill Gates published a new essay warning that the AI industry is crossing the safety lines it set for itself, and that nobody is preparing for what’s coming . At age 70, he also uses AI more than most people half his age, and he finds it enthralling, as you’ll hear on this week’s show, with highlights from our interview with him.
Along the way, we dig into his three proposals: new institutions for managing the transition, a category of jobs reserved for humans, and a tax on the use and purchase of AI and robots.

The change in his own tech usage: “I joke with people that I used to have Claude-like people that I would send email to, but they were so slow, and there were some topics they didn’t actually know. … It’s three a.m. I want to understand sodium batteries, and now there’s no reason to go to sleep. Here we go. Yeah, it’s crazy.”

How he uses AI specifically: “If you’re a curious person, this is a mind-blowing time. When I’m working on malaria, nutrition, my poor humans that I work with always get these long conversations from me, where I paste in — me, Claude, me, ChatGPT. Sometimes I do it if there’s three of us: Claude, ChatGPT and me, debating these things.”

On where personal agents are headed: “We will get to a point where you won’t buy things yourself. You just won’t. … You won’t go to those applications. You’ll just go to your personal agent. … From a productivity point of view, we are in heaven.”

What has surprised him: “I was shocked by ChatGPT, and I was shocked by Claude Code. Those are both things where I went, oh my God. … I did not expect that a statistical machine would essentially learn to read, and the idea that the code is better than human code. Those are two stunning thresholds.”

On writing this essay: “It’s very unnatural for me to think that innovation may be a net negative if it’s not managed properly. The more I wrote the memo, the more I was like, Jesus, we really need to get our act together here. Even though this may come across as negative, that’s the truth. If we don’t step up, the negatives will substantially outweigh the positives.”

What AI leaders say privately: “You’re in this perverse period right now where people in the AI industry who are willing to say that AI might have some negative effects are told, ‘Hey, you’re hurting our PR while we’re trying to raise trillions of dollars.’ … I know they’re all worried. Or all of them that I know, which is basically everybody but Elon.”

On losing control of AI: “The wake-up for the memo is that the bad stuff thresholds are all being crossed. Even lack of control that I thought would be many years from now, we’re seeing lack of control. … These are people who are super expert on the thing, going, well, maybe we won’t be able to control these things. What kind of risk have we chosen to run here?”

On how fast robots are coming: “What’s weird about AI is it’s better at doing jobs across the entire economy, including physical jobs when the robots come — which you can guess when that is, but my view is it’s only a couple of years.”

Is he still an optimist? “I don’t think being pessimistic is helpful. I do think, wow, this is sure an interesting time. I’m the guy who in my 30s thought people in their 50s or 60s didn’t understand anything. So it’s kind of bizarre if a guy who’s 70 comes and writes a memo that’s actually helpful. … But I am very concerned. And honestly, when you get people one-on-one, so are they.”

articles.title: Op-Ed: Washington’s Primary Election Results Underscore the Case for Proportional Ranked Choice Voting
articles.author: Zane Gustafson
paras: From Seattle to Spokane and everywhere in between, August’s primary results show an electorate yearning for more options, and proportional ranked choice voting is the way to make viable candidates from outside the two-party system.

Contrary to the blinkered two-party analysis in the Seattle Times , which explicitly excluded independent candidates and ignored major differences between Democrats, Washington primary voters showed they support three viable statewide political parties: Democrats (40% of the statewide Congressional primary vote), Republicans (35%), and an emerging left-wing party (20%).

For this analysis, I analyzed candidate websites for rhetoric and policy platforms to identify which candidates are running as establishment or moderate Democrats and which candidates are running on progressive or socialist platforms. The left-wing label includes members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) like State Rep. Shaun Scott, progressive Democrats like Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal, Brent Hennrich, and Kevin Fagan, and independent left-wing candidates like Kshama Sawant and Melissa Chaudhry.

These primary results are evidence of what is already known in Olympia: that the governing Democratic Party in Washington State is a coalition of at least two smaller parties. Or, as Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen put it on my podcast Ungerrymander America : “I’m already the leader of a multiparty coalition called the Democratic Party, that includes a broad range of people. From people who, if you could just get them to say what they think, identify as communists or socialists, to people who in a different time could easily have been Republicans, and everything in between.”

Though this emerging left-wing party is not yet formalized, candidates espousing anti-establishment, progressive, or socialist rhetoric and policies are finding support across the state. In addition to former Congressional Progressive Caucus chair Pramila Jayapal (WA-7), left-wing candidates received enough votes across Western Washington to prevent four incumbent Democratic Congresspeople from reaching 50% of the vote: Rick Larsen (WA-2), Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (WA-3), Adam Smith (WA-9), and Marilyn Strickland (WA-10).

Across the mountains in Eastern Washington's Fifth Congressional District, incumbent Republican Michael Baumgartner underperformed, receiving just 47.4% of the vote. The remaining 52.6% was split between mainstream Democrats, progressives, and independents.

Failing to win 50% of the vote means Baumgartner is vulnerable. But for challenger Carmela Conroy to win, she will need to build a cross-spectrum coalition that includes everyone from the 4.4% of voters who voted for left-wing candidates to the more than 20% of voters who voted independent. Conroy's coalition building efforts were helped by the full-throated endorsement of her by independent Nate Powell, who finished third with 16.5% of the primary vote.
Taken together, over one-quarter of primary voters voted for either a left-wing or independent alternative to the two-party system to represent them in Congress.
The same kind of multiparty dynamic is playing out in legislative races across Washington State.

First, contests in the 37th and 43rd districts show that Seattle has a two-party system of moderate/establishment Democrats being challenged by progressive Democrats and DSA-candidates. Both districts will send a DSA-member to the legislature, with the 43rd's Shaun Scott running unopposed for reelection and the 37th’s Jaelynn Scott winning an overwhelming 88% of the primary vote.

Both districts have contested races, with the establishment Democrat Sen. Jamie Pedersen favored to win reelection in the 43rd. On the other hand, left-wing challenger Kelabe Tewolde won more than 51% in the primary in the 37th. These results should not be interpreted as definitive victories for either the moderates or the progressives; the key takeaway is that there are two distinct factions competing across Seattle districts and the more left-leaning democratic socialist faction is making headway and establishing itself as a distinct political force.

This isn’t only playing out in Seattle. Left-wing candidates are making gains elsewhere too. In the redrawn 14 th district that stretches from Yakima to the Tri-Cities, incumbent Republican Rep. Deb Manjarrez received 51% of the primary vote, showing that the district will be competitive in November. In the race for second place, the labor and immigrant rights activist Ezequiel Morfin beat self-described moderate Tony G. Sandoval. To be clear, Morfin identifies as a Democrat. I categorize him as part of this emerging left-wing party because his platform centers working families and places his campaign in opposition to corporate donors and party insiders.

Meanwhile, voters in Eastern Washington are looking for independent alternatives. In addition to Nate Powell coming within 3% of second place in the Fifth Congressional District, the 6th Legislative District had independent Aaron Croft come within 259 votes of advancing to the general. Powell and Croft were two of five independent candidates in Eastern Washington endorsed by the Independent Veterans of America .

The concurrent and separate races for the two State House seats in the 6th LD show the appeal of independents. For seat #1, four Republicans combined for 57% of the vote while two Democrats received 42%. But just 50% of 6th LD voters supported Republican Jonathan Bingle for seat #2. Some 2,000 voters, 7% of the 6th LD primary electorate, voted Republican in one race then voted Independent in the other.

Take it all together and the shape of Washington’s multiparty politics comes into focus: the governing moderate to center-left Democrats fighting off a challenge from a left-wing party currently strong in Seattle and growing across the state; and a Republican Party losing relevancy in the State Legislature facing challenges from increasingly organized independent candidates.

Unfortunately, the structure of Washington’s top-two voting system is artificially keeping the two-party system in place and contributing to the widespread political cynicism that contributes to many people opting-out of voting. Voter turnout in the 2026 primary was just 37%, lower than the more than 40% turnout in midterm primaries in 2022 and 2018.

By implementing a proportional voting system, such as proportional ranked choice voting (RCV), Washington could send a multiparty delegation to Congress and have a formal multiparty politics in the State Legislature. This would help heal our political cynicism by providing voters real options beyond the two-party system.

Instead of a winner-take-all system like we have now, where the candidate with 50.1% of the vote wins and the other 49.9% of the district is left without, proportional RCV elects multiple winners in the same district. This means far more than 50% of voters will see someone they voted for win the election. For example, in a district where the top three candidates win, 75% of voters would be represented; in a four-winner district this goes up to 80%.

Individual candidates would still need to win at least 20% of the vote to be elected in a four-winner district. For a deep dive on the mechanics, see chapter 6 of my 2024 book Polemic for Democracy on the Ungerrymander America blog .
Finally, if implemented, the multiple winner function of proportional RCV makes gerrymandering functionally impossible , according to analysis by the Brennan Center for Justice.

Shifting to proportional RCV for electing members of the State House could be done through the normal legislative process, while changing the voting system for the Senate may require amending the state constitution ( Article 2, Section 6 ).

But, such a change may be unlikely to be popular among legislators bought into the existing two-party system. A final option if legislation for proportional RCV fails to gain traction in Olympia would be for Washington voters to bring an initiative to demand a better voting system that would give them more options.

The primary results show that at least 25% of voters are already putting their votes toward alternatives to the two-party status quo. And if there were a real chance to change the system? Who knows how broad the support for such an initiative might reach.

articles.title: Give Yourself Over to Absolute Pleasure at These ‘Rocky Horror’ Screenings
articles.author: Julianne Bell
paras: Tim Curry, known for his legendary performances in It , Clue , Home Alone 2, Legend , and The Rocky Horror Picture Show , died Tuesday night in his Los Angeles home. He was 80, and along with Dolly Parton, one of two gay icons to leave this world in a single day.

Like countless others, my strongest connection to Curry was through his portrayal of Dr. Frank-N-Furter—the “sweet transvestite from Transexual, Transylvania”—in Rocky Horror . As an (unknowingly) queer teen, wearing pleather and fishnets at midnight Rocky Horror screenings at the Admiral Theatre in West Seattle was a rite of passage. A few of my high school classmates were in the shadowcast, the costumed performers miming the action on screen. My mom went to screenings when she was young. Rocky Horror , and Curry, were always there.

Except—as my colleague, and fellow Rocky Horror devotee, Audrey Vann, lamented in our Complaints Issue last December —shadowcast performances seem to be nearly extinct in Seattle. Blessedly, for the sake of the youth, there are still a few. There’s no better time to do the Time Warp than where you are standing. Or, if you can wait, during the following shadowcast performances.

Riff Raff’s Street Rats is a Bremerton-based volunteer shadowcast troupe that performs at their home theater, the Tracyton Movie House, and at venues across the region, raising money for nonprofits across the Northwest. They have three shows planned in honor of Curry’s memory. See them tomorrow night (Saturday, August 29) at the Skyline Drive-In Theater in Shelton. Gates open at 7:30 p.m. Get there early for the 9 p.m. pre-show initiation ritual before the 9:30 p.m. screening. According to their website, audience “partici…… pation” is encouraged. The Street Rats next take the stage Saturday, September 19, at the Admiral Theater. Doors open at 9 p.m. and the show starts at 9:30 p.m. Their biggest Tim Curry tribute will take place at Olympia’s Capitol Theater on Saturday, October 3 , with doors at 11 p.m. and pre-show beginning at 11:30 p.m. before the film—a rare midnight screening. Prop bags will be sold separately outside the venue.

On Instagram , the Street Rats expressed their grief at Curry’s death. Says cast member Chynna: “Growing up in rural Idaho, there was very little support for the LGBTQ+ community. I had to hide who I was, who I liked, and what I wanted, until a beautiful man with a beautiful voice kicked in the door with platform heels. My world was rocked. To me, it did feel like being transported to another planet, and for once in my life, I did feel like I was coming home. Tim became a beacon of hope for me, a battle cry for everything I did that got me called ‘weird,’ and I am honored to still perform in the shadow of that greatness.”

Tacoma’s Blue Mouse Theater screens Rocky Horror every second and fourth Saturday of the month, with their in-house shadowcast, the BlueMouseketeers. On September 12, they’ll host a memorial for Curry . The cast will organize a small memorial altar outside the theater, and guests are invited to donate art, cards, or other small items in his memory. Concessions and prop bags will be available at the lobby. Doors open at 11 p.m.

“For decades, the Rocky Horror Picture Show has provided a space of community and belonging for people of all walks of life; notably, the queer and trans communities, and Curry has played a huge part in that,” the BlueMouseketeers wrote on Instagram . “In honor of Tim Curry, we ask you all to remember the movie’s message of ‘don’t dream it, be it.’ We can’t ever replace this loss, and it’s difficult to express in words the grief this community feels, but the Blue Mouseketeers are committed to carrying on Curry’s legacy and keeping this show alive for as long as we can.”

Another shadowcast, the Vicarious Theatre Company , performs at the downtown Regal Meridian 16 the first Saturday of every month. I couldn’t find any information about Curry tributes, but on the Regal website , a show is scheduled for 10 p.m. on Saturday, September 5.

Prior to Curry’s death, a few Rocky Horror events were already scheduled in Seattle for the Halloween season. Patricia Quinn, who played Magenta in the original film, will stop by the 5th Avenue Theater on Thursday, October 15 for the 7 p.m. Rocky Horror Picture Spooktacular Tour screening . The evening will feature a live shadowcast with the BlueMousketeers, plus a VIP meet-and-greet with photo ops and autographs. Obec Brewing will host an interactive singalong screening at 7 p.m. on Friday, October 30, while Unexpected Productions will put a live improv spin on the film each Saturday in October.
