articles.title: Everett Link Reaches Key Federal Approval Milestone
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The Federal Transit Administration (FTA) has put its signature on the draft environmental analysis for Sound Transit's Everett Link project, which would extend light rail 16 miles north from Lynnwood.

Board Vice Chair Ryan Mello shared the news at the Sound Transit board meeting Thursday, noting federal approval allows the project to tick off another milestone. Sound Transit is aiming to open Everett Link in two phases, with four stations up to SW Industrial Center tentatively set for 2037, and Downtown Everett tabbed for 2041.

"Last week, we received some outstanding news from our federal partners, as the Federal Transit Administration signed the Everett Link Extension Draft Environmental Impact Statement, clearing the way for a September 18th publication of that really important extension," Mello said. "This is a key milestone. It launches the public engagement period for Everett Link Extension, in which the region will be able to learn more about the current state of the project, and share their priorities for Everett Link Extension going forward."
The public engagement period on Everett Link will start on September 18 as soon as the draft Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) is released and must last at least 45 days by law.

The draft EIS will need to be finalized and converted into a final EIS, which will also require federal approval and another public comment period. With that hurdle cleared, Sound Transit could advance to final designs and break ground on the project.

Sound Transit is still waiting on FTA approval to release the DEIS for the much more complex Ballard Link Extension. Originally, that document was initially set to be released much earlier than the Everett Link counterpart. The agency blames "federal regulatory changes" since the second Trump Administration took office, with every additional month of delay on that project costing the agency tens of millions according to Sound Transit.
The release of Everett Link's DEIS suggests that not all projects are receiving the same level of scrutiny and headwinds at the FTA.

Sound Transit is hoping to wrap planning on Everett Link by the end of 2027, with construction anticipated to start in early 2031. That timeline makes the project somewhat less at the whims of the Trump Administration, which has yet to sign any transit grant agreements since taking office in 2025 – in fact it has sought to claw back several existing transit grants – even as it has been willing to eventually approve some transit planning documents. A new administration that could take over in 2029 may be friendlier.

Advancing the Everett extension has been a clear priority for the agency's 18-member board, under the banner of " completing the spine " from Tacoma Dome to Everett Station, a 62-mile corridor. This is especially true for the board's Snohomish County delegation led by Snohomish County Executive Dave Somers, who chairs the board.

Hooking over to SW Industrial Center is far from the most direct route to downtown Everett, but it does take the light rail line near Paine Field – which Snohomish County officials hope to grow into a secondary airport for the region —plus Boeing's sprawling manufacturing plant. This preference has led the board to rule out the cheaper, faster alignments along SR 99 or I-5.

Voters approved funding for Everett Link in 2016's Sound Transit 3 (ST3) ballot measure, but most projects in that package have run into significant planning hurdles. Back in 2016, Sound Transit had hoped to open Tacoma Dome Link in 2030 and Everett Link in 2036, while West Seattle Link was tabbed for 2030 and Ballard Link for 2035.
A 2021 ST3 realignment delayed timelines for most projects, with the pandemic taking a good chunk of the blame.

In May, the board overhauled ST3 delivery schedules in light of a $34.5 billion long-term budget gap. The "Affordable ST3 Plan" put forward by Chair Somers delayed several extensions, potentially scrapping some projects forever. However, Everett Link made it out relatively unscathed, with no further delays announced at the time.

The Tacoma Dome Link Extension is still officially tabbed for 2035 , but with Sound Transit not anticipating breaking ground until 2030, that could be optimistic. The construction phase on Sound Transit's light rail projects have generally lasted six years or more .

In contrast, the agency revealed last month light rail to Ballard could be pushed to 2060s without further action to find major savings or secure new revenue. The agency's best-case scenario would open the entire Ballard Link project from SoDo to Ballard in 2042, if it's able to close the roughly $8 billion budget gap that pushed it to table the Ballard and Interbay stations, while advancing the downtown segment.
The Everett Link project will need to keep moving through the process for its anticipated 2037 opening for the Paine Field segment to stay in play.

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.title: Right-Wing Radio Host Ari Hoffman Files Political Finance Complaints Against the Seattle Times
articles.author: John Stang
paras: Radio host Ari Hoffman of KVI AM 570 news radio fired the first shot Aug.18 in a barrage of complaints to the state government that allege “the legacy media” is cheating on Washington’s campaign finance laws.
His target? The Seattle Times and its opposition to a failed 2024 ballot measure to repeal a new industrial carbon emissions law.
He filed his complaint against the Times and its Climate Lab with the Public Disclosure Commission, which regulates political campaign finances in Washington.

On Aug. 24, Hoffman filed a second PDC complaint regarding the Times’ project homelessness coverage, which has at least two reporters funded by donations from homeless institutions. He claims this coverage improperly boosted a Seattle housing property tax levy in 2023, which successfully replaced an expiring 2016 levy.
Hoffman declined comment. “I do not give comments to anti-American antisemitic rags like the Stranger,” he wrote in an email.

Essentially, Hoffman’s Climate Lab complaint to the PDC claims that liberal groups sent money to the Times through the Seattle Foundation—an 80-year-old philanthropic organization that provides grants and investment money to a wide range of causes and ventures, including donations it funnels to the Seattle Times ’ Climate Lab project—so the paper would write stories and editorials to sway readers to vote against a 2024 ballot measure that would repeal the state’s new Climate Commitment Act (CCA). The CCA, a quarterly state auction of carbon carbon emissions credits to polluting industries which pays for numerous global warming mitigation programs, survived by a 62-percent-to-38-percent margin.
The Seattle Foundation and some of the Climate Lab donors also make political donations.

According to Hoffman’s complaint, The Seattle Times and donor organizations should be investigated for potentially violating Washington campaign finance reporting requirements by not reporting the financial value and sponsor identification for political advertising, expenditures, contributions, and in-kind support associated with opposing 2024’s ballot measure.

The complaint claims the Climate Lab, a team of four climate reporters whose 2024 coverage specifically addressed the carbon emissions credits law only a handful of times, differs from normal newsroom operations because it is funded through donations and not from the paper’s normal revenue.

Hoffman wants the PDC to interview the Times ’s Climate Lab reporters and editorial board members. Plus, he wants the commission to examine all of the Times ’s stories and editorials, as well as all finances and emails involving the Times ’s relations with the Seattle Foundation and its climate-related donors.
The Seattle Times and the Seattle Foundation both declined comment.
Hoffman, a right-wing commentator, does not present any specific details that prove that the Times ’s climate change coverage is not factually based, accurate, nor objective.
This practice of using donations to bolster news coverage has become more common among newspapers, whose revenues have dramatically shrunk due to advertising drying up

The Spokesman-Review is one such paper. Its longtime owners—the Cowles family—recently transferred ownership to a new Spokane non-profit corporation, Comma Community Journalism Lab. Comma’s list of donors is public .

Also, the Washington State Standard is part of States Newsroom , a nationwide non-profit collection of newsrooms funded by roughly 1,200 donations of more than $1,000 for it to cover state governments. Conservative interests have accused States Newsroom of liberal biases, which the national organization denies having. The liberal Hopewell Fund largely bankrolled States Newsroom from 2017 to 2019 until the organization got on its feet. Several liberal interests are among the national group’s donors.
The Washington State Standard has the biggest statehouse news operation in Olympia, and is a neutral workhorse whose stories are reprinted by several state papers.

Another relatively new Olympia news operation funded solely by donors is The Center Square. The conservative Franklin News Foundation (formerly the Franklin Center) funds The Center Square in numerous states. Most donors to the Franklin News Foundation are anonymous. The Center Square (formerly Watchdog) concentrates on business and tax issues, although it has stretched into other matters.

Philanthropy.org, a nationwide donation-tracking Web site, says that Project 42, a leading Washington conservative funding operation, donated $3.1 million to the Franklin News Foundation from 2021 to 2024.

Redmond hedge fund manager Brian Heywood leads Let’s Go Washington, which has three initiatives on the November ballot – banning transgender girls from girls sports, revoking the millionaires’ income tax, and a parental rights measure.

Heywood also helps control the pursestrings of Project 42, whose subsidiary Future 42 is a regular advertiser on Brandi Kruse’s podcast. Kruse is also an official “ambassador” of Future 42, which translates to being a very vocal supporter.

Meanwhile, right-wing podcaster Kruse says she soon plans to file PDC complaints similar to Hoffman’s against the Times , the Tacoma News Tribune , The Stranger , her former employer KIRO Newsradio, and the independent Black outlet Converge Media.

Kruse and Hoffman are not coordinating their complaints. “Ari Hoffman did that all on his lonesome. I learned about it after the fact,” she said about his first complaint in an email to The Stranger .

Hoffman’s and Kruse’s PDC filings are apparent payback for a group called Washingtonians For Ethical Government (WFEG) filing a complaint against Let’s Go Washington in May. That complaint alleged that the conservative initiative organization Let’s Go Washington has not properly filed campaign documentation related to Kruse’s podcast, unDivided, being a major supporter of the organization’s November 2026 ballot measure to ban transgender girls from girls sports.

The WFEG complaint alleges 159 instances of Kruse boosting the measure on her podcast from September 2025 to February 2026, plus two times she led political rallies on the same topic. The complaint alleges that Kruse’s support crossed the line from commentary to at least $345,000 in free advertising. Kruse still discusses this measure on her podcast several times a week.
The PDC recently decided to launch a formal investigation into this claim—roughly 90 days after it was submitted. A couple Seattle television newsrooms noted that launch .
On her Aug. 18 podcast, Kruse pointed to the PDC not terminating the May complaint, which she contended unfairly tainted her and Let’s Go Washington with a bad image.

She believes that the PDC is deliberately not resolving the May complaint by now. “The PDC’s decision to allow (the Washingtonians For Ethical Government complaint) to linger is a political decision,” Kruse said.

As the PDC investigates the complaint against Let’s Go Washington, it will have to parse legal and semantic differences between commentary and free political advertising. A 2007 Washington Supreme Court ruling that declares radio host commentary is not political advertising will also likely be a factor in the PDC’s investigation. The commission will also likely examine financial and organizational ties between Kruse and Brian Heywood, sponsor of the anti-trans Let’s Go Washington measure and two others on November’s ballot.

Kruse is angry that her podcast is receiving bad publicity from this matter because Let’s Go Washington is accused of the actual insufficient campaign reporting – with her podcast not being required to report to the PDC. “I have a First Amendment right to support any initiative I choose,”she wrote in her email.

On her Aug. 18 podcast, Kruse said she would “assemble an army” to be paid with her own money to compile detailed information on the advertisers, stories and finances of The Seattle Times , The Stranger , The News Tribune , KIRO News Radio and Converge Media to send detailed complaints to the PDC.

Meanwhile, Kruse wrote in her email: “I selected a wide array of media outlets to make a point: it’s not about politics, it’s about equal treatment under the law. If the PDC chooses to erode my First Amendment rights, then they must also go after those who are similarly situated – including dear friends of mine. Anyone who engaged in commercial advertising while also engaging in opinion on candidates or campaigns is impacted.”
After the first five complaints are filed, Kruse plans to continue submitting similar complaints regarding other Washington news operations.
“I will spend every waking hour burying the PDC in bullshit over this,” she said on her Aug. 17 podcast.

Kruse and Hoffman ally themselves with right-wing activist Jonathan Choe. The trio routinely participate in conservative political activities. Kruse also is paid to speak at Republican functions, and she campaigned for free for GOP gubernatorial candidate David Reichert in 2024.

Months ago, Kruse and Cho attended an Antifa roundtable at the White House where Kruse told President Donald Trump that her support for his second term made her feel more attractive—a remark out of sync with accepted press professionalism.

The three are co-plaintiffs in a federal lawsuit to be declared journalists so they can get access to the Democratic side of the Capitol’s House chamber in Olympia. They already have access to the entire Senate chamber and to the GOP side of the House chamber by various means. The judge in charge of that litigation told them that their chances of prevailing in that lawsuit are slim.
While this is technically a separate issue from the PDC matter, Kruse has loosely co-mingled the two in a few podcasts.

Editor’s note: The original headline of this story read, “Right-Wing Podcaster Ari Hoffman Files Political Finance Complaints Against the Seattle Times.” While Ari Hoffman’s show is available to us all in podcast form, he is a radio host.

articles.title: Seattle Transit Trivia Answers
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Thank you to everyone to joined Seattle Transit Trivia on Monday. After a competitive game, top scores are:

If you are one of top scorers, please check your email for information about the prizes. This post will share the correct answers for all 39 questions. If you missed the game on Monday but want to test your Seattle transit knowledge, check out the questions from Round 1 , Round 2 , and Round 3 .
Q1: How many transit agencies support ORCA cards?

Nine: Community Transit, Everett Transit, King County Metro, Kitsap Transit, Pierce Transit, Sound Transit, Washington State Ferries, Seattle Center Monorail, Seattle Streetcar. RandomNerd answered correctly first .
Q2: What was the first bus rapid transit line operated by an ORCA agency?
The Swift Blue Line opened in 2009. Henry Horenstein answered correctly first .
Q3: Which bus route(s) operated by an ORCA agency do not connect with any other bus routes from the same agency?
Pierce Transit Route 497 is isolated from the rest of the PT bus network. The route is a peak only service between Landland Hills and Auburn station. Henry Horenstein answered correctly first .
Q4: Which Sound Transit route has stops outside the Sound Transit taxing district?
Sound Transit Route 595 serves stops in Gig Harbor. Aaron Gu answered correctly first .
Q5: List each King County Metro route that is branded as an express service.
Metro’s once expansive network of express bus routes has dwindled down to just 5 routes: 9X, 17X, 21X, 28X, 193X. Aaron Gu answered correctly first .
Q6: One King County Metro RapidRide bus has a rear window. Which bus?
Bus 6000 has a rear window. This vehicle usually operates on the A Line or F Line. HZ answered correctly first .
Q7: Which Community Transit Express route does not stop at a Link station?
CT Express Route 907 travels between Paine Field and Stanwood. All other Express routes stop at a Link station. HZ answered correctly first .
Q8: When did the oldest transit vehicle still used on scheduled routes by an ORCA agency enter service?
The Carlisle II began passenger service on April 9, 1917. The boat is still used on the Port Orchard ferry route more than 100 years later. Senior answered correctly first .
Q9: Rank the following transit agencies from highest to lowest based on their June 2026 ferry/water taxi ridership: King County Metro, Kitsap Transit, Washington State Ferries.
WSF had 1,956,901 passengers, Kitsap Tranit had 127,204 passengers, and the Metro Water Taxi had 86,707 passengers. Aaron Gu answered correctly first .
Q10: How many ORCA card taps were recorded in 2025?
ORCA recorded 76,671,844 taps in 2025. Aaron Gu answered correctly first .
Q11: What was the first ferry route operated by the Washington State Department of Transportation (or one of its predecessors)?
Washington state began operating the Keller Ferry in 1930, 21 years before Washington State Ferries took over ferry routes in Puget Sound. Henry Horenstein answered correctly first .
Q12: In Fall 2025, how many average daily boardings did the busiest Metro bus stop have across all routes?

The Metro stop at 3rd & Pike (northbound) had an average of 2,950 boardings each day . The stop is served by routes 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 13, 14, 36, 70, 125, C Line, D Line, and E Line. Aaron Gu answered correctly first .
Q13: Which Link station is shown in the picture below?
The vertical concrete slats are a unique feature to Symphony station. Aaron Gu answered correctly first .
Q1: Which route operated the last scheduled bus trip through the Downtown Seattle Transit Tunnel?
Route 41 ran the last scheduled trip in the DSTT just after midnight on March 23, 2019. Henry Horenstein answered correctly first .
Q2: How many boardings did Everett Transit record on its free shuttles on July 4, 2026?

The free Everett Transit shuttles carried an incredible 10,192 passengers on July 4. To put that into perspective, the rest of the Everett Transit network had about 2,500 trips on the same day. Henry Horenstein answered closest without going over.
Q3: Rank the following jurisdictions from most to least based on the number of number of bus stops used by King County Metro in Fall 2025: Bothell, Issaquah, Kent, Redmond, Renton, Shoreline
The correct order is: Kent (306 stops), Renton (295 stops), Redmond (234 stops), Shoreline (222 stops), Bothell (79 stops), Issaquah (77 stops). No one got this completely correct.
Q4: Excluding Trailhead Direct, shuttle routes, and school routes, which King County Metro bus routes with at least one stop in Seattle have zero stops within 1000ft of a Link station?
Only three routes meet this criteria: Route 22 and DART routes 773, 775. Blumdrew answered correctly first .
Q5: The first double decker bus in Puget Sound entered service on August 1, 2007. What route did it first operate?
Community Transit rolled out their first double decker bus on Route 402. Scooby Doo and the Goblin King answered correctly first .
Q6: Identify one location (Link station and direction) in Seattle where Link shuttle buses use a stop not shared by any other routes.
Southbound Link shuttles at Rainier Beach station use a dedicated stop. Scooby Doo and the Goblin King answered correctly first .

articles.title: Idaho Law Protects Faith Healers. It Wasn’t Always That Way.
articles.author: Audrey Dutton
paras: In Idaho, parents who say their faith prohibits lifesaving medical care for their children can’t be charged with child neglect or manslaughter. Supporters of this protection over the years have included lawmakers who voiced support for “traditional” Idaho values.

But from at least the 1880s through the early 1970s, it was illegal for parents in Idaho to choose prayer over medical care when a child’s life was at stake, newspaper archives and historical documents show.

“Every parent of any child who willfully omits, without lawful excuse, to furnish necessary food, clothing, shelter, or medical attendance for such child, is guilty of a misdemeanor,” reads the 1887 edition of Idaho territory statutes , published before statehood.

The statutes included no mention of spiritual belief as a “lawful excuse.” Three years later, the state constitution explicitly put limits on Idaho’s freedom of religion. It would not excuse “acts of licentiousness,” polygamy or other practices “inconsistent with morality or the peace or safety of the state.”

It wasn’t long before the law came down on members of the Followers of Christ, a faith-healing sect that arrived in Idaho in 1899 and remains active in the state. From 2015 to 2025, the sect’s congregations in Idaho experienced 15 preventable deaths of children , according to ProPublica’s reporting.

Pearl Annis was a 13-year-old girl whose parents had moved from Oklahoma to Idaho’s Magic Valley in the spring of 1915 with at least one other Followers family. The Annises and their 13 children shared “a two-room shack,” a local newspaper reported. An officer and a doctor visited the home after neighbors voiced concern. They found Pearl in bed, fully dressed and on the cusp of death.

Her father, Lurid P. “Lewis” Annis, was arrested on a misdemeanor charge of refusing to provide medical attention. Pearl was taken to the hospital, according to the news story, and died there with what today would be described as septic shock from a bowel blockage. The newspaper, which didn’t appear to follow up on Annis’ criminal charge, called the Followers church “a religious cult” and Pearl’s death a consequence of “religious mania.”
News archives and historic records don’t say how many times Idaho acted on similar cases in the decades after.

But one legal battle over lifesaving care drew attention in the 1960s, as sickness made its way through a Followers family in a Boise suburb. The mother died in December 1965. Her 4-year-old daughter died the following June.

Days after the girl’s death, a judge ordered the state to take custody of her 10-year-old brother under Idaho’s child protection law. The boy was admitted to a local hospital with pneumonia, a complication of the measles. He spent days in critical condition but survived. The judge told the father that to regain custody, he would have to be willing to give the boy medical care as the law required.
A doctor testified that without the hospitalization, the child “almost certainly would have died,” a newspaper report said.

The father’s lawyer told the judge that his sect was rooted in “faith that God will heal the sick.” The law in the 1960s was clear, though: a parent had a duty to protect their child’s health, no exceptions. The judge told Samuel’s father: “The law governs conduct. Religion governs opinion.”
But the legal landscape was about to shift. It came with little public attention.

During a full-on rewrite of Idaho’s criminal code in 1971, the Legislature added a section that said the state could not bring endangerment charges against someone “who chooses for his child treatment by prayer or spiritual means alone.” Legislative records don’t make clear how the wording originated. The passage of another law one year later, affirming the “spiritual means” language and applying it to other crimes, has been credited to the Christian Science church, another Christian denomination with Idaho members.

(The Christian Science website says the church’s practice of “healing in the way Christ Jesus taught” is not “faith healing” and that members are free to choose any form of healthcare . The church also supported Oregon’s full removal of its faith-healing exemption in 2011.)

Faith-healing exemptions soon became widespread nationally. The trigger was the federal Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act of 1974 , which set out to standardize the nation’s child welfare system by giving states grants to more effectively investigate reports of child abuse.

The Department of Health, Education and Welfare interpreted the law as requiring states to have a faith-healing exemption to qualify for the grants — an interpretation that records from the time don’t explain.

Most states went along, and Idaho further broadened its exemption in 1976 to not only keep faith healers from going to jail if their children died, but also to keep their children from being placed in foster care solely for lack of medical care.

At the national level, the mandate lasted less than a decade. The Reagan administration adopted new regulations in 1983 that took a neutral stance on the subject, and several states in subsequent years rolled back their exemptions.

Colorado, for example, reverted to prosecuting faith healers as it would any other parent in 2001 following deaths in the Followers-adjacent sect Church of the First Born, including the death of a 13-year-old girl from untreated diabetes.
But Idaho clung to its special treatment for faith healers.

paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?

articles.title: The Best Seafood Restaurants in Seattle
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Seattle is synonymous with seafood, and anyone who visits from out of town naturally wants to know where the city’s best seafood is. But that’s a tricky question. There are some self-described “seafood restaurants,” but fish and shellfish work their way into nearly every menu around Puget Sound. This includes oysters on the half shell at too many happy hours to count, crab and geoduck served as high-end delicacies, and sandwiches where freshly caught salmon or tuna is the star ingredient. A “best seafood in Seattle” map would pretty much just be a map of Seattle. So consider this a sampler platter of some of what the city has to offer across several different styles of cuisine and price point.

paras: Often thought of as Seattle’s southern little sister, Tacoma has surged in population in the last decade, and Washington State’s third-largest city can definitely hold its own against its siblings when it comes to its food scene. From fried chicken and waffles in Lincoln to luscious bagel sandwiches in Edison City, from Vegas-style fine dining in rural Midland to the absolute ocean of Korean food in Lakewood, the dining options here are tremendous.
